8, 56.5 × 5.5 cm; *Gomola* script (from Vikramaśīla).
[1v] Homage to Vajraḍāka!
Having prostrated to the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*,
its division is being written down from the Guru for the correct recollection of someone else.
In the spaces that are insentient yet clear, in the non-expansive yet luminous,
in the universal abode of vajras, in the dissolution within the delightful realm of sentient beings.
The ground of the various vajras, abiding as a celestial palace, Pure together with space, without interval, and all-encompassing.
Regarding "the realms of sentient beings and the mind's delight" (sems can khams dang yid 'ong):
1.1 "In the spaces," and so forth—space is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*);
"the insentient" refers to earth.
"Transparent" refers to Varuṇa;
"unobstructed" refers to Vāyu;
"illuminating" refers to Agni.
"Viśva" refers to the universal lotus situated within the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). "Vajrālaya" refers to the universal vajra atop the universal lotus.

"Layana" refers to the peaked temple (*kūṭāgāra*) produced by the transformation of the four great elements—which have been moistened by streams of nectar generated through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of Vairocana, who arises from the *bhrūṃ* syllable seen upon the lunar disk. Regarding "sattvadhātāv": that very [temple] is the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) because it serves as the support for the *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs*.
Likewise, it is "delightful" (*manorama*) because it is composed of the five jewels.
This is what is meant: "situated within the palace inside the source of phenomena" (*dharmodayā*)—this is to be connected with the subsequent word "situated" (see 8a).
[He is situated] in the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel, within the realms of *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*;
in the mind, in the body, and in speech; in one, in two, and in the void of bliss.
Sentient beings, the vessel-world and the physical world,
the appearances of the earth and that which lies beneath it,
as well as the mind, body, and speech—
"Single, dual, and the bliss of space.
(1.2) He says "sattve vā" and so forth, because [the reality] abides even among both existent and non-existent beings due to its pervasiveness as the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"He" refers to [the state] within moving things.
"Bhājana" refers to the stable [receptacles].
"Loka" is an epithet for these two alone.
Explaining "sattva," he says "bhūḥ" and so forth.
Respectively, [this applies] to those situated in heaven, the mortal world, and the underworld.
"In between" means among these very [realms], other than the receptacle world (*bhājana*).
"In the mind," and so forth, refers to the mind, body, and speech of these very [beings].
"In one" refers to the aspect of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*), which is the pure form of these very [elements], having the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"And two," etc., refers to that which consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), the bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion.
"In space and in passion" refers to the aspect of the grasped (*grāhyāṃśa*), which has emptiness as its nature.
In the six, in the five, in the twelve, in the four, even in the worlds,
and throughout the entirety of the three realms— even in the nineteen [worlds].
Six, five, and two;
four, and all living beings;
and with one, twenty were not left out.
"Without exception throughout the three realms" (1.3):
"In the sixfold" refers to the six sense bases (*āyatana*) beginning with form (*rūpa*). "In the fivefold" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*).
"In the twelve" means in the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

"In the four" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Even in the nineteen" should be applied here as well; the meaning is that [it exists] in the eighteen constituents (*dhātu*) together with the person (*pudgala*).
Then follows the explanation of the vessel: "in the worlds. This is its specific definition: "the triple world in its entirety.
[It is found] in the father, in the son, in the mothers, and indeed both externally and internally.
In all women, in the Dharma, in all actions, and in that which is not the self.
Whether it be father, son, or mother;
whether external or internal;
or all the queens and the Dharma—
"From all [phenomena] and selflessness," and so forth.
The phrase "in the four" should be applied immediately after "father, etc. The meaning is: "in those very fathers and so on that are well-known in the world.
Regarding "external, etc.": by means of the designation "external" and "internal," he indicates precisely existence and non-existence.
"In all women" means that because all vidyās are the basis of bliss, he abides therein—this is the intended meaning.
"And in dharma" refers to blue, yellow, and so forth.
"And in all actions" refers to the characteristic activities such as coloring and so on, pertaining to these very same [objects] like blue and the rest.
"Non-self" (*anātman*) refers to the body of a deity that is empty of the ordinary physical form. Thus, it is said:

"In the fruit, in the cause called the effect, in the goal, in the possessor of the vajra which is the means, likewise in the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and in the non-arising of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)."
"Effect, cause, and activity; the object to be accomplished, the means of accomplishment, and the vajra;
likewise, the ālaya-vijñāna."
The dharmadhātu and the unarisen.
1.5 *Phala* means in the *phalahaivajra*;
*hetau* means in the *hetuhaivajra*.

Regarding the term "called the effect" (*kāryākhya*): this is an epithet for these two alone. He states this very point as "the means and the possessor of the means within the goal" (*sādhye sādhanavajriṇī*).
Alternatively, the goal (*sādhya*) is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and the means (*sādhana*) is the method for that very [bliss].
Now, indicating the *ābharaṇa* (?), he says "tathā hi" and so forth, in order to show the two states of the very object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), consisting of the defiled and the pure:
"In the *ālayavijñāna*, characterized as the abode of all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
in the *dharmadhātu*, having attained the nature of non-abiding."

Regarding "non-arising": it is that which is devoid of production from any cause other than the moment of the appropriating consciousness (*upādānacitta*). [It resides] in the realm of sentient beings and the realm of space, in that which is selfless yet perceived as a self, in the non-existent, in the absence of appearance, in Sukhāvatī, and in the triangle.
The expanse of space and one’s own basic nature,
selflessness and what is called "self," neither a thing nor not a thing.
"Within the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) and within the space-realm (*khadhātu*).

Regarding "within the realm of sentient beings": it refers to the *ādhāra* (basis), because it is the support for the seeds of that which is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. And regarding "within the space-realm": it is so called because it nourishes practitioners through the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because it is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, it is "non-self.
Because it exists as a self that is itself devoid of both [aspects], it is designated as "having the notion of self" despite being non-self.

The explanation of this term "non-self" is "in the vibhāvas. It is called *vibhāva* because in it the entities such as the grasped and so forth have departed (*vigata*). The plural number is used because it is worthy of worship.
The explanation of "possessing the notion of self" is "non-existence" (*anābhāva*); it is not "existence" (*abhāva*) because it exists in the form of the disappearance of the grasped and the grasper.
It is in *Sukhāvatī* because of the protection (*rakṣaṇa*) of the limb that is bliss, characterized by the knowable.
It is in *Trikonaka* because of its triangular form and its nature as the earth.
In the passionless, fault-free, stainless,
and purified samādhi, which is waveless and experiences true bliss within.
Born from the [Dharmadhātu],
free from defects, stainless, having conquered evil, and by nature devoid of the turbulence of the passions;
"In the end, there is the awareness of the bliss of peace.

(1.7) Because passion and the other afflictions are absent therein, it is "stainless" (*araja*). These very points are explained through further elaborations and their subsequent elaborations, such as the statements beginning with "in those free from defects" (*vigatadoṣeṣu*).
Because it is free from all conceptual construction, it is "waveless";
because its nature is one-pointedness of mind, it is "in meditative absorption";
and because its nature is the experience of bliss consisting of the aspect of the apprehended, it is "internally experiencing true bliss."
Always abiding in the supreme, delightful secret, which is the self of all, the being consists of all Buddhas; he is the Vajrapañjara of the Ḍākinīs.
In the Secret, Supreme, and Joyful [Tantras]...
the Bodhisattva who pervades all Buddhas.
In the *Vajrapañjara* of the Ḍākinīs: because it is to be concealed from those who are unfit vessels, it is "secret" (*rahasya*);
because it is supreme, it is "supreme" (*parama*).
It is "delightful" (ramye) because of its loveliness;
it is "the self of all" (sarvātmani) because this very [Self] is the self of everyone; it is "eternal" (sadaiva) because of the permanence of its continuity throughout all time.
The connection is with the word "abiding.
To the question "Who is he?", he says: "consisting of all Buddhas," and so forth. Because he has the nature of all Buddhas, the meaning is that he is "composed of them," namely Mahāvajradhara.

Furthermore, because he is constantly engaged in the welfare of sentient beings (*sattva*), he is a "being" (*sattva*). And because he acts as a prohibitor against the outward departure of the *ḍākinīs* such as Nairātmyā and others, he is like a "diamond cage" (*vajrapañjara*), hence a "diamond cage" (*vajrapañjara*).
That Blessed One, the Self-Existent, is the sole presiding deity;
from the Great Vajra whose nature consists of five hundred thousand [stanzas], he proclaimed the five mandalas.
"This is the self-arisen Bhagavān;
the sole lord of the gods,
the universal self, eternally abiding."
Regarding the statement that the Lord Vajradhara spoke of five mandalas in the *Pañcalakṣa*,
[the author] asks what he did after remaining [there] and says: "Asau" and so forth.
"He" refers to the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he is self-arisen (*svayambhū*) due to the absence of a cause. He is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) because of his possession of the six qualities, such as sovereignty and the rest.
By virtue of having the nature of the *dharmakāya*, he is one and without a second. Because his essence consists of the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, he is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*).
"He spoke"—this is the grammatical connection.
"Five mandalas" means the pentad of mandalas;
[this refers to] the Vajrin...
Vajradhara and Hita,
as well as Vajratejas himself,
Padmanartteśvara, and...
This very point he states with the words beginning "of the Vajrī" and so forth; it is easy to understand.
In the mandala of the Vajra-Ḍākinīs...
The White Thief, the Vetālinī,
Ghasmarī and Pukkasī, the mountain-dweller, the outcaste woman, and the young maiden. 1.11
With the words beginning with “Gaurī,” he speaks of the deities of the maṇḍala:
“In the Vajrānkuśa maṇḍala,
there are twenty-four parched [deities].”
Holding a bell, a wheel, and a hook,
along with flowers and so forth— this is the section on the offerings. 1.12 “Flowers and so forth” means flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes.
In the mandala of Vajrasūrya,
there are Sūryahastā, Dīpā,
Ratnatārā, and Vidyunhastā.
Regarding "lāsyādyāḥ" [in the *Asye la Sogs*]: these are lāsyā, gītā, nṛtyā, and hāsyā. [From the *Padma Chos ’Byung Lcags Sgrogs*:]
In the mandala of the dance of the *khyud ma* goddesses,
the border regions consist of the *gling bu ma* and so forth,
through the application of one's own costume and attire. 1.14
"Vaṃśādyāḥ" means the flute, the lute, the mṛdaṅga, and the muraja drums. In the royal maṇḍala, there are the vajra, the gate, the iron chain, and the crossbar.

Sgrol ma (Tārā) and Gos ’dzin ma (Pāṇḍaravāsīnī), and likewise Locanā and the others at the intermediate directions. Regarding "Locanā and the others": they are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsīnī, and Tārā.
With their left hands forming the heart-mudrā, the fist-mudrā, and the threatening gesture, they are of various colors and exceedingly radiant.
All those vajra ḍākinīs abide with their left legs extended; at their hearts,
they form the threatening mudrā with the left hand.
"Various colors" (*nānāvarṇā*) means they are endowed with colors such as white and so forth. Furthermore, their colors are to be understood according to the *saṃhāramaṇḍala*.
Excessive delusion and great delusion...
extremely hateful and greatly hateful,
well known as Gaurī and the others.
From the great delusion of extreme ignorance, one should especially grasp at things such as dry wood and the like.

"Atimoha" and so forth: for sentient beings, "extreme delusion" (*atimoha*) is an excessive delusion, a confusion of mind; for the sake of removing that, there is "great delusion" (*mahāmoha*), which means great enthusiasm. Therefore, the meaning is that they have that as their intrinsic nature. "By extremely radiant great light...
"...extremely passionate great passion..."
Extremely radiant and intensely luminous,
renowned as the sun and so forth,
arising from great passion.
...in the Dharma-maṇḍala of the *pa* syllable and so forth.

1.18 "Atiteja" means that the excessive brilliance (*tejas*) is the pride of sentient beings. To remove that, there is "great radiance," which is vigor (*ojas*). This is to say it is powerful. The sense is: by means of that, [it is] by way of that intrinsic nature.
"Atirāga" is intense attachment to sensory objects. To remove that, there is "great passion" (*mahārāga*), which is great attachment or commitment. Therefore, the sense is that they have that form.
From great envy and great obscurations...
the swift-moving goddesses such as Cāndālī and the rest.
The Victorious Lord Phanta (Phan-pa) brings about the exhaustion of all delusion (*moha*).

1.19 *Maherṣyā* is a mental factor that prevents others from engaging with one's own possessions. Because he covers, conceals, and suppresses that [envy] with great effort (*mahatā yatnena*), he is the "Great Obstructor" (*mahāvaraṇa*), that is, one of great energy (*mahotsāha*). Therefore, the meaning is that they have that as their intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāva*).
"...the cataract of conceptual construction... | "O Great King Vajrasūrya, you who dispel the darkness of conceptual construction."
The great Rta mgrin 'Dod pa chen po bestows enlightenment upon those possessed of desire;
he is one who avoids other vehicles. 1.20 *...anyayānavivarjakaḥ |
Vajrasattva, the great king, who arises from the wisdom of Akṣobhya.
O Vajra Swift-Farer of Great Ferocity,
who has utterly abandoned all other vehicles,
Great King Vajrasattva!
The source from which the wisdom of bliss arises (mi bskyod ye shes 'byung ba'i gnas), verse 1.21:
"Other vehicles" refers to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and so forth.
"Vajrasattva" refers to Akṣobhya.

Regarding "the source of the knowledge of Akṣobhya": the meaning is that he is so called because the supreme arising of the knowledge of emptiness, which is Akṣobhya, occurs [within him] despite the conceptual constructions of the afflictions (*kleśa*). He is the destroyer of the five obscurations for the sake of inviting the inexhaustible world.
"In order to invite the inexhaustible host of living beings, he is the destroyer of the five obscurations.
(1.22) Regarding "jagat" and so forth: *jagataḥ* refers to the multitude of sentient beings.
"In the inexhaustible gnosis of emptiness" means for the purpose of invitation and for the sake of bringing [the deities] face-to-face.

"The destroyer of the five obscurations" means that its nature is to strike down— that is, to kill— the obscurations to the gnosis of emptiness belonging to the five cognitions that arise from the conceptual constructions of self, sentient beings, objects, and formative factors.
The samādhi called "The Vajra of the Tathāgata’s Purity.
Hatred, delusion, pride, desire, and avarice arise in beings.
"Because of the *bsdud phyir* (for the sake of gathering), one should hold many forms of vajras upon one's own wheel.
(1.24) Regarding "the stingy ones" (*matsariṇaḥ*): it refers to those who are miserly.
"In many ways" means fivefold.
"Knowing that gentleness is not appropriate toward those who are extremely wicked and fierce," thus [said] the Great Vajrin...
One should not apply pacification toward those who are extremely fierce and violent;
this great Vajra-holder is omniscient.
For those who are attached to extreme emptiness, may they become vajra-born by their own power. 1.25 *atiśūnyaprasaktānāṃ, for those who are attached to extreme emptiness.
For the sake of purifying the ignorance of those who hold to ascetic practices and vows that do not exist,
one becomes the Vajra Perfected Buddha. 1.26
"Of those who are excessively attached to emptiness" means of those who contemplate that "everything does not exist.
"The state of perfect buddhahood" means the nature of Vairocana. "Those who are intensely possessed by pride," etc.
He causes the pride of living beings to be exhausted;
he is the sovereign Vajrasūrya himself, who destroys the darkness of great pride. 1.27
Having abandoned what arises from attachment to awakening,
whatever sentient being brings about happiness, through that attachment,
supreme awakening is accomplished.
Become the sovereign of the lotus family;
those who abide on the path of omniscience yet travel by another way—
In order to bestow supreme enlightenment upon these beings,
you are the Lord Vajravega himself. 1.29 Whatever sense faculty may function as a path, that very thing [is so] by its own nature.
By means of the yoga of supreme absorption, one should carry [the visualization] consisting of all the Buddhas.
Whichever sense faculty is the path itself,
one proceeds into the very nature of that [faculty] through the yoga of supreme benefit.
"May I become the essence of all Buddhas.
(1.30ab) He speaks of the practice with the words "whatever... whatever," etc.;
"whatever" refers to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.

It may enter the state of the path of the sense faculties; one sees, hears, smells, tastes, or touches. "That and that"—the meaning is that all those [objects] are [perceived] by way of their own-being (*svabhāva*), in the form of their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and not as something transformed.
This is done through supreme concentration, with a mind that is intensely absorbed.

"Consisting of all Buddhas" means that one should carry or visualize them as being composed of the five ḍākas, as appropriate. For, by whatever state the minds of men are joined, [so do they perceive].
Through that, one attains identification with it, just as a crystal assumes the form of everything reflected within it.
By whatever means and by whatever entity beings apply their minds,
through that, they come to possess its very nature.
The various forms [of the deities] are like a treasury of jewels (sna tshogs gzugs nor).
1.31 To the question, "How is this possible to accomplish?", he says: "By whatever means," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
"By whatever means of discipline sentient beings are led to the state of being disciplined..."
In each and every way, one should perform the teaching of the Dharma.
By whatever means and by whomsoever beings are to be disciplined,
through those very forms, they are brought to maturity.
Now, the explanation of the Dharma will be given.
1.32 He speaks for the sake of sentient beings with the words "by whatever means" and so forth: "Downward, downward;
sentient beings, arisen from the mind-vajra, possess various natures."
The mind, through the conceptualization of a self...
[arisen from the Vajra of Mind],
possessing the nature of various sentient beings.
"The mind is made black by the stains of worldly beings through their own conceptualizations.
(1.33) Showing the manner of the teaching, he says: "Cittavajra," and so forth.
"Of diverse natures" means having diverse lineages (*gotra*). "By the conceptualization of a self" means by views such as that of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, with every effort, one should purify the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*).
When the mind is pure, there arises happiness that removes the poison of all afflictions.
By thoroughly subduing [the mind] from below,
one completely purifies the vajra of the mind; the purity of the mind is bliss.
It steals away all the poisons of the afflictions (1.34).
Regarding "bliss": it is the nature of that which is to be accomplished; it is the maṇḍala-circle whose essence is great bliss.
If emptiness were the means, then Buddhahood would not come to be.
Because the fruit and the cause are not different, emptiness is not the means.
If emptiness were the method,
at that time one would not become a Buddha,
because the result is not other than the cause.
The method is not non-emptiness;

[it is so] because of non-difference (ananyatvāt), that is, because of similarity. For those who have fallen away from the [correct] views and are searching for a view of self—*381A*—[the method is taught].
Emptiness was taught by the Victors for the purpose of eliminating the grasping at a self.
In order to reverse the attachment to a self held by those who hold erroneous views and those who seek a view of a self, [the Buddha taught:]...
The Victors have taught that emptiness is the means known as the mandala-circle, the vow of bliss;
through the yoga of the identity of oneself as the Buddha, Buddhahood will be attained before long.
Therefore, the mandala is called the wheel;
skillful means is the vow of bliss. Through the yoga of the pride of being a Buddha,
One will swiftly attain Buddhahood itself. (1.37) The Teacher possesses the thirty-two marks and the Lord possesses the eighty minor characteristics;
therefore, one should accomplish the goal through skillful means, and [visualize] the Teacher in embodied form.
The Teacher possesses the thirty-two marks;
the Lord is endowed with the eighty minor characteristics;
therefore, he is to be accomplished through skillful means.
"Now, [he is] embodied by means.
(1.38) "Embodied as the Teacher" means the Teacher, resplendent with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*), together with the members of the mandala.
This concludes the first chapter, titled "The Entrance of Beings through the Magnificent Excellence of All Aspects."
The first chapter, titled "The Entry of Sentient Beings," in which all aspects are supremely peaceful.
Thus ends the first chapter. || 0 ||

The Yoginī is the Vajrapañjara, the delightful samaya offering;
she has been thoroughly commanded by the retinue. 2.1

"Attained by the three worlds" means one who teaches for the benefit of the three realms. "Ritual worship" refers to the materials for worship as appropriate, according to the various types of universal monarchs.
[This] should be offered to the Vajra-holder.
I offer garments to the Buddhas,
likewise incense to the Supreme One,
and food and drink to the Lord of the World. 2.2
With offerings made by the GOS, upon the supreme horse:
"These are the sublime commitments;
having performed the vajra offering,"
"Causing all who possess the vajra to rejoice" (2.3) means by means of the transformations of vajra-worship; that is, by means of the specific worship just described.
O Vajra born from the smoke-colored [syllable].
Offer white sandalwood to Phanpa,
red sandalwood to the Lord of the World (Lokanātha),
and Kashmiri sandalwood to Vajraprabha. 2.4
All those kings of the seven [realms],
through this supreme application of fragrance, [offer] this scent arisen from the *hūṃ* vajra.
"One attains the state of a sublime Buddha.

2.5 "Gandhaṃ hūṃvajrasambhavam" means that the fragrance arises from the transformation of the seed-syllable and the emblem. The meaning is that it should be offered to the King of Horses (Saptirāja). "Offer cold water to the Vajra."
To Amṛtavajra,
to Vajrasūrya,
likewise to Lokanātha, and to Viśvabhadra. 2.6
One should thoroughly examine all the kings of *ṛta*,
O Vajra-holder,
with the vajra of "Kye."
A black dog with short legs appeared;
Mallikā and Mālatī always offered flowers to the Buddha.
The supreme, stainless,
vermilion-colored lord of the Śṛṅgī [flower] should be applied to the illuminator (the fire).
2.8 The lord of the color red is the water-born [lotus].
I offer the red Bandhu flower to Patale,
The lotus dance-mudrā to Padmanarteśvara, And the supreme horse to Vajrin. (2.9)
The Vajra-holder is three cubits;
the Buddha-maṇḍala is four cubits;
and the Illuminator (Prabhākara) is five cubits.
Padma Garwang is the sixth;
likewise, there are seven Iron Kings.
[They are] the food of Vajrasūrya.
From the supreme iron hook of the *lam du*,
and from the sleep of the Lord Buddha, 2.11,
there is great bliss and the mastery of dance.
At the time of fully seizing the ground,
one should place it in the form of a vajra, accompanied by the sound of music such as lutes.
I shall thoroughly accomplish my own yoga:
the blue Vajreśvara,
like the moon, water-crystal, and the Great Sage.
The flower born at Mkhar phyin is red; Avalokiteśvara is the red lotus; and the path of the horse is the mārgadatta.
The supreme colored powder of the five precious gems (2.13).
Then the Blessed One, the Great Vajra-holder, dwelt in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "Subduing the Bhūtas of the Vajrapañjara of the Ḍākinīs" (2.14).
[He who is] the essence of the seed-syllable of Samantabhadra.
I am the seed of Samantabhadra, who perfectly distinguishes the authentic commitments.
"Having the nature of the seed-syllable of Samantabhadra" means he is born from the syllable *hūṃ*. He is like the blue Indra, possessing four arms, and is the Great Bhairava.
The body of the beautiful wrathful one bears the lords of the elements;
with his right hand,
he holds the Lord of the Family itself.
With the left hand, one should not touch; by means of the application of the mudrā with both index fingers, it is grasped. 2.16 *kalitaṃ tarjanīdvābhyāṃ mudrāprayogataḥ |*
The two hands are joined in the mudrā; standing firmly with the left leg extended,
he strikes fear into beings with his slightly bared fangs.
"The supreme ornament of the garland of heads" (2.17):

"It is formed by the two index fingers through the application of the mudrā. Having performed the *vajrabandha*, having linked the two ring fingers like a chain, having pressed the nails of the middle and little fingers with the thumb, and having bent the two index fingers, one should hold [the mudrā] at the heart; this is the mudrā.
"The head bound in half-tie..."
One should meditate on the crown of the head;
one will achieve the subjugation of spirits. 2.18 *The nāginīs and yakṣiṇīs...
Many yakṣas and bhūtas,
yakṣīs, nāgīs,
and human women as beautiful as goddesses—
The practitioner will certainly achieve success.

2.19 Regarding *nāginīs* and *yakṣiṇīs*: having attracted a *yakṣiṇī* by means of rays from the syllable *kṣīṃ* seen upon a golden pedestal or similar object, and having caused her to enter therein, one should visualize the *yakṣiṇī* as yellow in color, holding a white parasol, with her head trampled by Bhūtaḍāmara; thus she is accomplished. Likewise, a *nāginī* is [attracted] by means of the syllable *naṃ*.
The seed-syllables for the human maiden and the celestial maiden are the first letters of their names. The mantra is:
*oṃ bhūtadāmara bhūtapati ākṣobhya kṛtiṇa sarvabhūta preta piśāca siddhaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then the Great Vajra, the Vajra-holder, dwelt in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) known as the Powerful Vajra Pavilion of the Ḍākinīs.
Abiding in the samādhi of great power, one should cause the eight nāgas ...
[to emerge] as an eight-petaled lotus,
and then rain down great showers.
Visualize an eight-petaled lotus;
upon it, one should arrange the eight nāgas.
By applying oneself with great power, 2.22.
"Lotus" means an eight-petaled lotus with the color of the nāga of its own direction.

"The eight nāgas" means: Ananta, blue, in the east; Vāsuki, white, in the south; Takṣaka, red, in the west; Karkoṭaka, red, in the north; Padma and Mahāpadma, pale-white, on the petals of the southeast and southwest; Śaṅkhapāla, yellow, in the northwest; and Kulika, of variegated colors, in the northeast.
[Then] one should properly press the drums.
From the great power of the *cāmuṇḍī*, one should cause a stream of water to fall; it is black in color and very bright. 2.23
Terrifying those who are terrified,
with eight arms and four faces, he makes the sun and moon his vajra seat.
"By his hands he holds the lord of nāgas. (2.24) "Seated upon Tārkṣya and Vajra" means he has the seat of Garuḍa born from Gaṃ.
Having performed the interlacing with two *HŪṂ*s, one should utter the *PHUḤ* mantra.
Reciting the mantra beginning with "PHU," one should cause the syllable "HŪṂ" to enter within,
and the syllable "PHAṬ" should be appended at the end. 2.25
"Interlaced with two *hūṃ*s" means that at the end of the garland mantra, one should place the syllable *phuḥ* between two *hūṃ*s; the sense is as follows: *hūṃ phuḥ hūṃ phaṭ*.
"The face of the first is black, the second is indeed Candraprabha."
The third is like the color of gold;
the fourth is described as being red itself.
Adorned with ornaments of snakes on his limbs.
Adorned by Vajrasattva,
for the sake of causing the nāgas to send down rain, one should thoroughly accomplish the one of great power. 2.27

"...one should reveal the reality of Buddhahood. Then the Vajradhara King, who maintains the nature of all Buddhas, the speaker of the Vajra Pavilion, shall clarify the reality of the Buddha. 2.28 Having made the vajra-lotus [gesture]...
One who has eaten the ornaments of the seasons, one who possesses wealth by drinking vajra-water—
it is this very Buddha who knows [this]. 2.29
In words such as *cumbita*, the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*).
In words such as *vajrapadma*, the nominative case is to be understood in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*). [This occurs] in the *Śuddhāvāsa*.
The place of realization is a great site,
perfectly filled with all the Buddhas,
pervaded by vajra jewels.
I shall explain that which has occurred: 2.30.
In the delightful city of benefit, the ḍākinī Vajra-lagu-rgyud (Vajra-Chain).
One should bind all the great Buddhas with iron shackles and stone fetters. (2.31) "Because of great affection" means because of a great craving for spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
"By the Sphoṭa-Vajrī" means by means of a chain whose nature is as indestructible as a vajra. "One will leap into the Joyous Realm (Tuṣita) and attain the desires of the Buddhas."
The Victorious Lord Maitreya gazes with his eye of primordial wisdom;
bound by the vajra chain, 2.32.
The assemblies of kings should be bound; whoever does not grant the siddhi should be summoned after being bound with a rope. 2.33
Vajra White Noose, the Great One; Vajra Hook, the Thief;
Vajra Chain, the Vetālī.
With the vajra and bell, O Ghasmarī,
one brings the Buddhas under one's control.
2.34 At that time, by means of the fourfold group of the four ḍākinīs...
If the siddhi is not granted to one who delights in recitation and meditation, then at that time,
the four ḍākinīs—
"The Buddhas accomplish through forceful means" (2.35). This refers to the previously mentioned group of four, beginning with Sūryā.

Herein is the sequence: for those who have turned away from granting accomplishment, in the first six months one should perform an invocation preceded by worship; in the second, one should strike them at the heart with a hook; and in the third, one should perform the ritual of pinning (*kīlana*) preceded by summoning them by force (*haṭha*).
Now, within the *Vajradhārapatividyādharīvajrapañjara-tantra*, I shall provide the authentic explanation of the five hundred thousand [stanzas]. 2.36.
There are one hundred thousand maṇḍalas of the Buddhas, and likewise one hundred thousand for those possessing the Vajra.
One hundred thousand [verses] are the Vajrasūrya;
one hundred thousand [verses] are the Vajradharma; fifty thousand [verses] are the Vajra.
Through five thousand subduers of spirits, the fivefold activity is fully expanded;
through these five, he is the Buddha-Dancer himself.
By thirty thousand [verses],
the *Kuru-kulle-vyākhyāna* is [completed];
by the remaining fifty thousand, [the rest].
This is the sequence for all tantras. 2.39.
Five hundred thousand [verses] of the Vajraḍāka were written down. 2.40.
Then the wise Vajradhara dwelt in the samādhi of the Buddha’s dance, the Vajrapañjara Ḍākinī.
2.41 ...the Buddha’s dance;
by the vajra of the Buddha’s dance, the means for awakening for those possessed of passion.
In order to gather those sentient beings who are deeply attached to dance and song,
the Buddha, acting as a dancer, performs his play.
By the Buddha Naṭarāja Vajra, enlightenment was accomplished through passion. 2.42 Then the Vajra-holder emerged from the application of the handful of flowers.
Then Vajrapāṇi appeared,
perfectly adorned with a flower basket,
for the benefit of all sentient beings.
The commitment (samaya) therein shall now be explained.
Regarding the passage beginning with "then it issues forth" (*atha niścarati*),
the term "Vajrin" (*vajrī*) is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).
From the withdrawal of the arms and so forth, one should understand [the sequence] beginning with the *cakrī* and *ratnī*.

Regarding "vajrāñjali" and so on: in both hands, by means of the syllable *A*, one visualizes a moon mandala; therein, by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, a white vajra; and one should visualize the fingers in the form of vajras. With a handful of flowers at the head, while prostrating with the words "Homage to all Tathāgatas," the meaning is that one should offer oneself.

In this dissolution maṇḍala, the dissolution of the four gatekeepers is Acala; the dissolution of the maṇḍala deities and yoginīs of Śāśvata is Locanā; [the dissolution] of the yoginīs of Vajrasattva is Māmakī; likewise, [the dissolution] of the yoginīs of Lokeśvara is Pāṇḍarā and Tārā; and [the dissolution] of the yoginīs of Saptirāja and Vajrasūrya is as follows. The intended meaning is that the dance should be understood as being performed by all the maṇḍala deities indeed.

As many sentient beings as there may be, subsumed within the category of "sentient beings," whether born from an egg, born from a womb, born from heat and moisture, or born spontaneously; whether they possess form or are formless; whether they are non-percipient or percipient—I shall establish all those sentient beings in the state of Mahāmudrā.
Having thus explained the great commitment, 2.44.
The protector Akṣobhyavyūha appeared and utterly reviled the Teacher, who was endowed with the wisdom that protects all beings. 2.45
O, you whose vow is called *hūṃ*,
you are the Great Sage with the Bow;
I am the one named the Glorious Power of Compassion.
"Are you not one whose power is invincible? 2.46 Is it that you have taken a vow? You are the Brahmin Sages."
O glorious Vairocana, you are free from fire and desire; why do you ask, "Is this your *samaya*? 2.47.
"O Lord of the Mnga'-bdag, Khading Khyen, what is your name? I am Padma Garwang Pal; you are the dancer and the assistant comedian. (2.48)
O you whose oath is called *trām*,
you who are fierce and steal away the heat,
I am named Vajrasūryaśrī.
How could your form not be that of a corpse? (2.49) What is your so-called "vow"? You are empty space by nature.
The *ṅam* is the swift-moving Vajra;
you are the horse that goes to the other side. 2.50 Do you maintain the samaya and compassion?
"O beautiful merchant woman, AE MA CHANG!
I am the immovable one, MĀKĪ.
Will you take me to your father’s city? (2.51)
"O you whose samaya is peace itself, are you a woman who holds to deceit and guile?
I am not; I am the goddess Locanā."
If you are a spy, you are full of agitation. (2.52) What do you have to say for yourself?
Do you claim to be truthful, or are you merely a great lecher who speaks of prostitutes?
I am the goddess named White,
whose complexion is as white as jasmine;
are you the great sovereign of the sacred commitments?
"Are you not the messenger of the Noble Lady?
My name is Sgrol ma with a squinted eye; my eyes have been destroyed. (2.54)
The patron Mig-yon-dag is wealthy and glorious;
thus, it is well because of being free from shame.
Without freedom from shame, one is not a Buddha.
"Quickly state what is inconsistent with what has been seen. (2.55) Then,
the Vajra Eye spoke these words of his own accord, surpassing even [the words of] censure.
Vajrasattva is great hatred;
the Sage Vairocana is delusion; the Lord of the World is attachment to desire. 2.56.
The one who acts as the vajra-light-maker is the "Sna-rdo-rje";
the one who accomplishes all meaningful purposes is the "Don-yod-skyon"; the five guides possess faults. (2.57)
Whether born from an egg,
born from a womb, born from heat and moisture, or born from a miraculous transformation;
whether possessing form or being formless—
That which is born from a womb, and that which is born from a sprout—
by saying "I shall make all beings Buddhas," you spoke these words first.
Once you yourself have become a Buddha,
how will you act as their Victorious Lord? For that very reason, you spoke what is false.
O Lord of Mṅga', why have you not said this? "If you deceive sentient beings, what would be yours? Buddhahood itself—how wondrous and marvelous! (2.60)
Whether the Lord of Death is great or not,
the harm of others’ wheels,
the consecration, the mandala, and the fire offering—
One who is always sporting with me, endowed with mantra and meditation, [attains] the auspicious and the peaceful. 2.61.
I shall sit before you, and there I shall not speak falsely. 2.62.
The Master, the Five Buddhas, and the Four Goddesses.
The Immovable One reproaches himself;
within the very site of the mandala palace, the Buddha performs the dance of play.
The dancers of the Buddhas perform their dance through the three realms, by means of the roots or the ornaments of impurity.
In the delightful city of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), with faith and joy...
(2.64) *dharmodayapure raṅge*... In the delightful city of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).
By means of songs of the vajra commitments,
by the practice of the vajra steps,
and finally with the sounding of clay drums and so forth, 2.65.
The reality that thoroughly bestows Mahāmudrā is here kept as a profound secret;
according to the command of Vajrasattva, [it is thus].
One should protect [the site] by means of intense exertion. 2.66.

This concludes the second chapter, titled "The Chapter on Various Songs, the Sound of Musical Instruments, Dance, Entering into Discipline, Causing Rain to Fall, and the Greatness of the Immovable Self. || o ||

Then King Vajradhara, abiding in the *vajrapañjara* (diamond-enclosure) samādhi, should utter the *mahābhūtabali* (great elemental offering). Regarding the phrase "abiding in the *vajrapañjara* samādhi": it means abiding in the *hevajra* samādhi.
One should visualize eight lotuses situated in the center of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). *NAM MKHA'I KHAMS KYI DBUS GNAS PAR,
PADMA 'DAB BRGYAD BSGOM PAR BYA.*

One should visualize Indrāṇī on the eastern petal; one should place Yamāntaka in the south. (3.2) "Situated in the center of the space-element" means situated in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). "The eight lotuses" refers to a red eight-petaled lotus.
Chu bdag (Varuṇa) is on the western petal;
in the north, one should draw Nor sbyin (Vaiśravaṇa);
in the southeast is Byin za chen po (Mahābhairava) himself.
Likewise, one should contemplate the non-dual boundary as wind, which is without abode;
in the northeast is the Lord of Beings.
Candracchattrā and the others,
as well as the noble Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita,
and the Mahābrahmā.
Abiding in the realm of Tuṣita free from strife,
becoming a great king,
and exercising mastery over the miraculous transformations of others.
Those who dwell in the abodes of Tuṣita,
those who reside in pure realms,
and those who abide in Sukhāvatī;
Those dwelling in Ogmin (Akaniṣṭha), those in the world-system of Marīcimat,
and those dwelling in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
One should cause them all to abide upon the summit;
as for their entering into the source of phenomena (dharmodaya),
it is through the causes of power and the protection of the conch.
Likewise, Anantaratnākara,
Sthāvara, and Kulika,
Mahāpadma, and Padmabhadra.
The gods, humans, hell-beings,
and sentient beings are below the source of phenomena (dharmodaya);
from the syllable Oṃ, Brahmā and the other deities arise.
With "Hūṃ" from attachment and so forth,
and "Āḥ" from the cause of power and so forth,
she possesses two hands and one face.
The deities of the upper [realm] are great white ones;
Indra and the others are similar to black ones;
the causes of power and so forth are great red ones.
Possessing the complete transmission of all the vidyās equal to her own, her hands joined with a vajra and bell,
she stands upon the seat with her right leg extended.
I seal [them] with the mudrās of Brahmā and the other [gods]; with the vajra, I perform the hundredfold offerings and so forth; and with the causes of power and so forth, I dance as the self.
All are born from the three families;
having summoned them by means of a white woman,
the female thief is bound with a rope.
Bind the tongues with cords,
strike them with pestles,
and then offer worship and present the water for washing the feet.
One should perform the purification offering with this mantra:
Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
Then, one should offer the scattered and poured libations.
With this mantra, request the deities to depart:

Oṃ vajrasattva samaya-maṇupālaya | vajrasattva tve no patiṣṭha | dṛḍho me bhava | sutoṣyo me bhava | supoṣyo me bhava | śāśvato me bhava | ānurato me bhava | hrīdayamme ādhitiṣṭha | sarvasiddhiṃ me prayaccha | sarvakāryeṣu me cittaṃ śreyaḥ kuru hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ | bhagavān sarvatathāgata-vajra...

Then the King Vajradhara, the Ḍākinī Vajrapañjara, abiding in the samādhi called "The Opening of the Vajra Name," spoke the mantra: *MĀ ME MUNYTSĀ BADZRI BHA WA MAHĀ SAMAYA SATVA ĀḤ MUḤ*. This is the "Opening of the Vajra Name."

"Abiding in the vajra-name samādhi" means that one should assign names corresponding to the respective families (*kula*) to the Buddhas and remain with the mind concentrated precisely upon that. Passion (*rāga*) is Amitābha; hatred (*dveṣa*) is Akṣobhya; delusion (*moha*) is Vairocana; commitment (*samaya*) is Amoghasiddhi; the being (*sattva*) is Vajrasattva; and the jewel (*maṇi*) is Ratnasambhava. At the time of the Name Empowerment, the disciple himself should be empowered.
Through the empowerment of the vajra name,
one is a Buddha in this very life.
Hāsavajra, Lāsyavajra, Śrīvajra, Līlavajra, Pramuditavajra, Pramuditāṅkuravajra, Padmavajra, Padmāṅkuravajra, Ālālāvajra, Padmaśaṅkhavajra, Jñānavajra, Cintāmaṇivajra, and Anaṅga.

The vajra of passion, the vajra of the sprout of wisdom, the vajra of the sprout of compassion, the vajra of supreme joy, the vajra of intense blissful joy, the vajra of Avalokiteśvara, the vajra of bestowing, the vajra of space, the vajra of wisdom, the vajra of the perfections, and the vajra of desire are the mudrās in the pure abodes.

These are the vajra names of the accomplished *candālīs*. As for the women, they are as follows: Vajrasattvā, Vajrayaṣṭī, Vajrāmoghasiddhā, Vajranairātmyā, Vajralocanā, Vajradākinī, Vajragaurī, Vajramāyā, Vajrajvālā, Vajravetālī, and Vajra...
Vajrāveśā, Vajravetālī, Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrāvartā, Vajramālā, Vajralāsā, Vajrahāsā, Vajrāliṅganā, Vajrasūcī, Vajrapadmā, Vajrasambhavā, Mahāvajrā, Vajrarāgā, Vajratārā, and Vajraghaṇṭā.

Dang, Vajralāsyā, Vajrakhaṇḍarohā, Vajradūtī, Vajrasaṃcālanī, and Vajravicitrā—these are the names of the ḍākinīs. Then, those who bear the names of the Tathāgatas: O Vajra, Vajrasattva, Mahāvairocana, Svayambhū, and the wrathful Vajrāralli Śoṣaka; likewise...

Yang is the wrathful Vajra himself; he is the union of the method of vajra-nectar and nectar, as well as Heruka and the power of compassion. He is the eternal one, the Vajra of Ignorance, Vairocana, and the Protector of All. He is the Illusory One, then the Lord of Oṃ, renowned as the Vajra Body, Kṣitigarbha, Great Ignorance, and Yama.

Yama, the Lord of Death, and likewise the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; he who is renowned as the Buddha, Vajrasūrya, then Ratnapati, and likewise Ratnarāja himself; Vajraketu, the Great King, Vajramāra-nirghātana, and Ālokakara; Hayagrīva, Lokanātha, and Vajradharma.

He is renowned as Avalokiteśvara, Padmanarteśvara, Rāga, and Lokanātha; as the Excellent Horse, Aśvarāja, and Saptarāja; then as Lakuṭīrāja, Samayavajra, and Paramāśva; likewise as Karmavajra himself, Amogha, Siddhārtharāja, and Vajravega.

PA'O. Then Vajrasattva, the Vajra-holder Vijaya-vajrapāṇi, Anupama-rasasama-susukha, and Paramādya-mahāsukha; Rāga-dveṣa-moha, and the Samayasattva Maṇi—these are declared to be the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), the accomplishers of liberation through desire (*kāma*). "Accomplishers of liberation through desire" means that they are the accomplishers of liberation by means of the five types of desire.
The third chapter, titled "The Marks of All Tathāgatas. || O ||

Regarding the term *hūṃkāra*: it refers to Vajrahūṃkāra. Regarding "the mudrā" and so forth: the mudrā is to be explained immediately hereafter. Through that [mudrā], there is victory, which is the overcoming of others. One is established in that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is one-pointedness of mind. The "mudrā-sign" (*mudrācihna*) is the sign that is the mudrā itself. As for the body, however, there is the hand-mudrā (*karamudrā*); thus, by means of the *hūṃ*-vajra, there are the vajra, wheel, and so forth, for those whose hands and other limbs have been purified. Likewise, from the instruction, there are the mudrās of the feet, the gaze, and so forth. Regarding the "speech-mudrā": on the tongue is a white vajra produced by a white *hūṃ*.

"From the recitation of the mantra" means from the recitation of the Nirodhakrodha. "But in the mind, the sign emerges" means that having mentally produced and fashioned the sign—such as the tongs and so forth—it is precisely that same [sign] even in the meditation maṇḍala; thus he says, "that very same. "The tongs in the right," and so forth, is all easy to understand. "The local commitment is spoken of as the ḍākinī" means it is perceived. It is not perceived because the body of the deity and so forth has been made manifest; the sense is that it is not perceived because the nature of emptiness is difficult to fathom. *Vajra-hṛdayābhisambodhi* (The Manifest Enlightenment of the Vajra Essence)
The first is the *Viniścaya-rāja*, the second is the *Māyā-viniścaya*,
and the third is the *Vajranṛtya*.
The Fourth is the Examination of Various [Matters]; the Fifth is the Examination of Vajra;
the Sixth is the Great Powerful One.
The examination of the Immovable Lord of Intent;
the eighth is the examination of the Form (?);
and the nine are the ḍākinīs of the Kuru-kulle family.
Chapter Eleven: The Examination of Discipline;
Chapter Twelve: The Examination of Siddhis; Chapter Thirteen: Vairocana.
The Thirteenth Tārā Parīkṣā,
the Fourteenth Vajravārāhī,
and the Fifteenth is of Great Splendor.
The Sixteenth: An Analysis of Selflessness;
The Seventeenth: Yamāntaka;
The Eighteenth: Hūṃkāra.
19. The Chapter on Sarasvatī;
20. The Examination of Homa;
21. The Consecration.
The analysis of the great mandala is held to consist of twenty-two [chapters],
and the analysis of the torma consists of twenty-three.
The twenty-fourth is the preliminary preparation;
the twenty-five are the clear realizations; and the twenty-six are the seals (mudrās).
The twenty-seventh [chapter] on the Twenty-seven Activities;
the twenty-eighth [chapter] on the Nāgas;
and the examination of the Lord of Dance (Nṛtyeśvara).
It is explained in the *Thirty Verses on Examination*, which consists of thirty verses; it is by way of the number thirty that [the three thousandfold world system] is [described].
The great ocean of the five hundred thousand tantras of the ḍākas and ḍākinīs—
this is the [teaching] of the Lord Vajradhara.
The tantra is taught extensively as the *Āma*;
it is the *Pañcalakṣahevajra*,
which completely upholds the essence of purity.
Thus spoke Vajradākinī;
this is the definitive meaning of the tantra.
O, Vajrayoga Tantra!
First, the Victors taught [the Father Tantras], and subsequently,
the Yoginī Tantras were taught in order to embrace women as well.

"Bhagavān, how is it that there is a withdrawal from conceptual proliferation? During the Fortunate Aeon (*Bhadrakalpa*), if the lifespan of bodhisattvas and ordinary beings becomes short, how will they maintain [the teachings]? How will they hear them? How will they contemplate them? Bhagavān, how is it that the lifespan of ordinary people becomes short?"

The Vajradhara commanded: "For the time being, those who become preceptors will incur root downfalls; those who are practitioners will engage in the ten paths of non-virtuous action; those who are ordinary beings will take the lives of living creatures; and those who belong to the assembly of women will be attached to sensual desire."
Thus it is transformed; therefore, not all tantras have been taught in detail.
Then, having heard the vajra speech of the Vajradhara of all the Tathāgatas, the Blessed One was pleased and, filled with joy, spoke these words:
"O Vajra Arisen from Great Compassion!"
In charnel grounds, on riverbanks,
in groves, and in uninhabited villages,
he bestows accomplishments upon those who offer service.
The delightful array of forms born from the lake,
the reliquary stūpas with deep chambers,
and beneath the short, submerged pillars—
I bestow the siddhi of Buddhahood in the marketplace,
in the very midst of the market stalls,
and in every kind of shop.
Vajrasūryadṛḍha,
you who bestow accomplishments upon those who offer service and honor.

In the house of a liquor-seller, amidst the intense binding of the *glu gar* dance, I, Padmanartaka, bestow accomplishments upon those who offer service. Whether constantly moving swiftly on foot or occasionally traveling along the road, I am the steadfast horse of meaningful purpose; the vajra accomplishments are above. Then, the Blessed One, the Great Vajrin, [is accompanied by] the Dakini Vajrapañjara-mudrā.

Having entered into the meditative absorption of the *Vijaya-samādhi*, the mudrās and hand gestures (*mudrā-lakṣaṇa*) are correctly explained. From the *Examination of Body, Speech, and Mind*: One should understand the three types of mudrās: The hand gesture belongs to the body; From the recitation of mantra comes the verbal mudrā; The sign belongs to the mind. That itself is the mandala of meditative concentration. In the right hand is the *śuṣka* (dry) [mudrā].

Likewise, with the left hand, she makes the threatening mudrā (*tarjanī*). O *Khaḍgaḍākinī*, do not fear! She removes the burden of the malevolent ones. In her right hand she holds a noose (*pāśa*); she binds and summons the malevolent ones. This is to be known as the noose. With the left, she makes the threatening mudrā against the malevolent ones. In her right is a circular seal (*mudrā*); she desires to lead away the malevolent ones. This is always explained as the circular *dol*. With the left...

Making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*) with the right hand while holding a hook, one intends to summon the malevolent spirits; this is explained as the Vajra Hook. With the left hand, one makes the threatening gesture toward the Māras; the right hand is the Sun (*sūrya*), which completely dispels the darkness of delusion (*moha*). The left hand is explained as the Fire (*agni*); it is called the Vajra Sun. The right hand holds a vessel for the fire, and likewise the left.

The threatening gesture (*tarjanī*)—this is explained as Vajrāmarī; she destroys the cataracts of conceptual construction. In her right hand she holds a jewel, bestowing gifts upon sentient beings; in her left she holds the threatening gesture. This is proclaimed as Ratnatārā. Lightning is in her right hand; she destroys the water-bearing clouds of conceptual construction. She should be known as Vidyutkarāmarī; likewise, with her left hand she holds the threatening gesture.

In the right hand is a lotus; the passion for the lotus is to be expressed. With the left, she holds the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*); this is described as the *ḍākinī’s* lotus. In the right is the lotus of the *bhaga*, where great bliss expands. On the left, she holds the threatening gesture; this is described as the downward-facing *dharmodaya*. In her right hand is a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*), which binds all through attachment to awakening. On the left...

Not holding the threatening mudrā, she is called Vajraśṛṅkhalā; desiring to embrace herself with the bonds of the Buddhas’ grace, she who is perfectly accomplished through passion for awakening is explained here as Vajrāliṅganā. Holding a chain in her right hand, she is the protectress of all primordial wisdom; holding the threatening mudrā in her left, she is called Vajraśṛṅkhalā.

Holding a *vīṇā* in her right hand, having taken up primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), she is the Cutteress; holding the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in her left, she is called Vajravīṇā. Holding a door-bolt in her right hand, not abandoning the arising of primordial wisdom, holding the threatening gesture in her left, she is called Vajratoraṇā. Holding a mirror in her right hand, she is the very protector of the queens who resemble herself; holding the threatening gesture in her left—

The female holder of the *mduzba* is called the lower vajra-vessel; she is the assembly of the sublime ḍākinīs of all the Buddhas. For the sake of perfectly accomplishing the five ḍākinīs, he spoke the Ḍākinī-tantra. Then, having heard that vajra speech of the ḍākinīs, all those bodhisattvas were struck with wonder and addressed the Blessed One, the Seizer of the Mudrā.

"Is this the seizing of the mudrā of the samaya of death? Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the bodhisattvas: "O Blessed Ones, bodhisattvas, there is a prophecy concerning the world-system called *Prabhāsvarā*, known as the *Vajranirdeśa*; this is it. It is in the language of Debehayasagamane."

In this language, it is conceptualization; because it is established as the practice of the all-pervading void, this is renowned as the *Ḍākinī*. Then, when all those bodhisattvas heard these words, joy and wonder arose within them, and they addressed these words: "O, how marvelous! This *Ḍākinī-tantra* is the ultimate among all tantras, easy to understand and easily realized."

It is difficult, and it is both knowledge and ignorance itself. Then, all the Vajra Tathāgatas, such as the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and the rest, spoke these words in order to exhort the minds of the bodhisattvas: "O Blessed One, regarding all these bodhisattvas here in this *Vajrapañjara-tantrarāja*, how [should they relate] to the yoginīs and the ḍākinīs?"

[This is] the summary of [the teachings on] the [Bodhisattvas]. The Bodhisattvas, beginning with Maitreya, requested: "By means of the five gates, I shall deliver infinite beings, such as those born from eggs, from cyclic existence. When Vajradhara spoke thus, preceded by such a vow for supreme enlightenment, why then [do you speak of] killing living beings and abandoning one's beloved consorts? How is this to be viewed?

In order to gather together the retinues of the various classes and the queens, the *Ḍākinī-tantra* is explained. It is a concise text with extensive meaning, a means for bliss that brings clarity to those of inferior intellect; it is certain to be the heart-essence of all tantras and the most excellent of mantras. This is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called the "Definitive Expression of Vajra. This is the explanation.

Instantly, the Yoginī Nairātmyā herself, having first performed worship through dance, spoke this of her own maṇḍala: "If I were to abandon the Buddha Vajrasattva, or even Vajradharma and Hayagrīva-Vajraravi, they would not attain accomplishment; yet I myself am generated in the form of the Mother of all Buddhas. Of them..."

O Beautiful One! In that regard, I am the *siddhi*. Through my favor, the practitioner attains the vajra *siddhis*: eye-salve, foot-ointment, the lower-accomplishment of the sword, the pill for moving through the sky, invisibility, alchemy (*rasāyana*), the state of a *vidyādhara* universal monarch, and the summoning of noble maidens. Thus it was spoken in many various elaborations.

"What should be done here? Abandoning the self is certainly not achieved; there is no enlightenment and no meditation. Yet, whoever constantly remembers the self, constantly recites and contemplates, recites the mantra garlands, and meditates upon my body—if they view it as being like an illusion or like a dream, then through the stages of profound meditation, they shall see me face to face."

From the *Bar 'gyur*, the *Pratimā-prayoga*: One shall bestow the siddhi of that [deity] through the supreme union of the vajra and the lotus. For one who grants all desires to me through the yoga of great bliss, what need is there to mention other embodied beings? By meditating on the single sun and through the yoga of the vajra offering, the siddhi of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is bestowed; of this, there is no doubt.

Having transformed oneself into Heruka and visualizing one’s own consort, I shall be pleased with those great yogins who desire me—those who possess the five qualities of sensual pleasure, who are full of joy and delight, and who delight in songs, dances, instrumental music, and all the bliss of every desire.

With various ornaments and finery, with drinks of various flavors, with garments of various patterns, and with ointments of various fragrances—whosoever constantly lies with me, to them I grant the accomplishment (*siddhi*). Abiding in the state of Mahāmudrā, my desire has become [fulfilled]. Oṃ ā āḥ ai aiḥ au auḥ ri rī li lī ae aai ao aau ām svāhā. Whosoever is exhorted by this...

In the hands of those sons of the Victorious Ones who perform the ritual service, the bliss of the illusion of a woman remains perfectly present. One should bestow Vajrī in the east; in the southern direction is the one with the form of Gaurī; in the western direction is the Water Ḍākinī; in the north is the Vajraḍākinī; and having placed her in the center, one should visualize her within the maṇḍala together with the essence mantra.

The mistress of that attendant is beautiful; she has two faces and one mouth. She is adorned with a curved knife and a severed human skull, wears a tiger-skin garment, has three eyes, and her hair is tied upward. She is fully decorated with the five mudrās. At the eastern gate is Mahāśvetā; at the south is Caurī; at the western gate is Vārī; and likewise, at the north is Ghasmarī.

Rā’o is in the northeast; Bukkasī is in the north; at the boundary of the quarrel (the southeast) is Ri khrod ma; in the direction of the rākṣasīs (the southwest) is the Caṇḍālī; in the west is the Gyuṅ mo. These are to be given without boundaries. Whoever practices this meditation intensely—no one is able to steal away the glory that has reached the palms of their hands. All of them are likewise black in color.
Above Rab tu ston pa (Prakāśa), there is the great wrathful goddess Śrī, accompanied by dance, holding a khaṭvāṅga in her left hand.
Then the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, abiding in the samādhi called the Supreme Joy of the Vajrapañjara Ḍākinīs, perfectly explained the initiation of the vidyā.

"Abiding in the samādhi of supreme bliss" means that because it is the cause of the disciple's supreme bliss, the five empowerments are "supreme bliss. In that samādhi, one is established in one-pointedness of mind. "The empowerment of the consort" refers to the five empowerments. By the water of the consort, the person, and all eight vases...

"By thoroughly meditating on the Vajra Mind, one should perform the empowerment of the Vajra-holder through contemplation. (*svavidyā* etc. This means by means of eight vases distinguished by the *bodhicitta* produced from the union of wisdom and method. It should be understood that the all-purpose vase and the victory vase are also to be included here. "The Vajra-holder" refers to Akṣobhya. "By the cultivation of the Vajra Mind" means by the meditation on the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*).
Having thoroughly meditated upon Vajrasūrya,
one should bestow the crown ornament there;
having visualized that all have been bestowed previously, one should contemplate it.
From the *Vajrapada-yoga*:
"The great nine-pronged vajra should be formed with one's own hands at the heart."

The disciple is made the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) and is empowered as Vajrasattva. "Sarvam" refers to the implements such as the song and so forth being visualized. "By means of the application of the vajra verses" refers to the recitation beginning with "The empowerment is the great vajra," and so on.
By means of the empowerment of the Buddha-Vajra,
you are empowered this very day;
this is the state of all the Buddhas themselves.
For the sake of accomplishing excellence, one should visualize the Vajradhāra embraced by the supreme goddess Tārā,
who holds a whip.
Holding the vajra and ringing the bell,
the Vajra Master should confer empowerment:
*Oṃ vajradhīpati stvām ābhiṣiñcāmi tiṣṭha vajrasamaya stvām*.
Having visualized the disciples as Vairocana, one should confer the empowerment by means of their names:
*Oṃ vajrasattva stvam ābhīṣiñcāmi vajranāmābhiṣekataḥ*. "O, [Name], Vajra!"
May all beings everywhere become like me;
may they each become Heruka themselves,
for the sake of the arising of the primordial wisdom of the Buddhas.

"The nature of phenomena is pure. To explain the essential nature of the water and other consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), he says: "Whatever appears," and so forth. Whatever [appears], such as water and the like—even though it is said to have the form of Akṣobhya and others—nevertheless, its fundamental nature is Heruka; this is the intended meaning. "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to external things or the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).

"From which" (*yad*) means from Heruka. "By the method of all-encompassing application" (*sarvopayikavidhānena*) means the ritual arrangement (*vidhāna*) of all-encompassing requisites for the mandala; the meaning is that they are offered according to the rules through the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) that [all things] are like an illusion and so forth.
"This very [mantra] is the nature of all Buddhas;
it rests in the hand of Vajrasattva,
the firm and disciplined Vajragarbha."
You too must always uphold this: Oṃ Vajra-tathāgata-siddhi vajra-samaya tiṣṭha samayas tvām āśo haṃ tvāṃ dhārayāmi hīḥ hīḥ hīḥ hīḥ hūṃ.
All [should be performed] with a single supreme [intention].
By means of constant, unsurpassed worship,
bestow the Vajra-discipline upon the disciple; thereafter,
[transmit it] from hand to hand.

"By means of all unsurpassed offerings" refers to the outer, secret, and reality (tattva) offerings. "From hand to hand" means from the hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*) into the hand of the disciple. "The Bodhisattva without beginning or end, the Great Joy of Vajrasattva."
Samantabhadra, the self of all,
the master of the master of Vajragarbha;
furthermore, bestow the bell upon the youth.
The vajra bell known as "Born from the Perfection of Wisdom," for the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings.
"This is proclaimed as following the radiance of the wisdom of all Buddhas;
it is what the Victorious One has described as supreme enlightenment."
You too must always uphold this;
having bestowed all the breaths of life,
you yourself shall become Śākyamuni.

Having granted the prophecy to the great disciple, [the text] says, "Taking up all consolation," and expresses the consolation of the disciple with the verses beginning with "Having seen" and "Having entered."
You have no fear of death or sorrow, nor likewise any illness or fever;
you possess the Great Vehicle of great bliss.
"O son prophesied by me from this [teaching], Oṃ Āḥ Śoḥ Hāṃ Vajrakaro Mi-stvām Vajrasattva Tathāgata!
Having been delivered from the miserable states of existence..."
For the sake of the siddhi of perfect existence,
O accomplished one,
you shall likewise become a Tathāgata whose name is Vajra.
Thus the Blessed One proclaimed the commitment (*samaya*) of the empowerment of Mahāmudrā.
Then the Blessed One, the Great Vajra, the Teacher who reveals the Samādhi-vajra, uttered the one called the Samaya-vajra and spoke these words:
"Samādhivajradeśaka" means the teacher of the samādhis beginning with the Initial Yoga (*ādiyoga*). "Niścārya" means having placed it in the mind. "Vajrasamāyākhya" refers to the three samādhis.
Make offerings to the Vajra Gurus and purify the seven branches;
then,
generate the bodhicitta.

"One should perform the seven purifications" means: confession of misdeeds, the vow of non-committing misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication of merit, taking refuge in the Three Jewels, generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and relying upon the path. "Having generated the mind of awakening" refers to having performed the meditation on emptiness. This is an elliptical expression; one may also meditate on the "Vajra Cage" and so forth. "The visualization of the source of phenomena" (*dharmodaya*) means that within the protection wheel, one should perform the visualization of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) which has arisen from the transformation of the Vajra-Hūṃ syllable and other such forms.
Having visualized the abode of the Buddha,
one should meditate on the five aspects; first,
one should visualize the person, and then—

"The emanation of the wheel of ḍākinīs" means that therein, within the *dharmodayā*, upon a double lotus and a double vajra. "Fivefold aspect" refers to the meditation on the moon, sun, and so forth. "The primordial person" refers to those who have become the cause. "The circle of ḍākinīs" refers to the host of deities beginning with Gaurī.
"The gandharvas enter into equipoise."
One should recollect Khubar;
one should be exhorted by the Boundary Goddesses with the words "gandharve tv iti. Within the three syllables placed between two red *hoḥ* syllables:
Having exhorted the Guide of the Wheel, one should contemplate the three vajras abiding in the three places— the eyes and so forth, as well as ignorance and the rest.

Regarding the phrase "the leader of the wheel," it should be understood that [he] arises. One should place the term "trivajra" [at the three centers]: Khecarī at the heart, Bhūcarī at the throat, and Pātālavāsinī at the crown. One should meditate on the three syllables HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ upon the moon of the heart. Then, the subsequent sealing with vajras and the entry of the wisdom-beings.
Empowerment is the lineage of the vidyās,
as well as the tasting of the nectar and the offerings of the eight goddesses.

This is the "Praise of the Guide of the Wheel" (*vajrānurāgaṇa*). The intended meaning is that, for the sake of manifesting the wheel of *ḍākinīs*, one must bring satisfaction to the two vajras—wisdom and method—in every mandala.
[One should] empower through self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
One should meditate on the six branches of yoga; thereafter,
furthermore,
by means of the sequential stages of the ritual of the samaya.

"Furthermore, one should correctly characterize the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)," meaning blue, yellow, and so forth. Regarding "self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and so on, this occurs in the *Karmarājāgri-samādhi*. One's own meditation is one's own gnosis; by means of that, there is the consecration of others, which is the application of each to their respective gnosis. "The signs" refers to the five signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
First, the form of clouds...
The second resembles smoke;
the third has the appearance of a firebrand; the fourth is like a brightly blazing lamp.
The fifth is constant luminosity;
it is like a cloudless sky,
and that is the cause of omniscience.
"Attainment is imminent. Regarding "having the form of a cloud":

that which is as subtle as a mustard seed or a mirage becomes the form of a cloud due to its state of being a single mass; this is the [form] of Hevajra. "Resembling smoke": resembling a fragment of the appearance of smoke, this is [the form] of Śāśvata. "Having the form of a firefly": similar to the light of a firefly, this is [the form] of Sūrya. "A blazing lamp": having the form of a blazing lamp-flame, this is [the form] of Padma. "Always luminous," and so forth: having the form of the sky with its clear light, this is [the form] of Ghoṭaka. Or, it may be for each one individually in sequence.
In all five types of signs as well, it should be understood that it is only the form of the Buddha that appears in the manner of a mirage and so forth. "Subsequently, like the form of an illusion,
the dream changes moment by moment."
The three realms, including both the moving and the non-moving, are accomplished without exception or remainder;
"afterwards" means when this accomplishment has been achieved.
"In all world systems,
for as long as there are those with vajra bodies,
may they possess the intellect of the aggregate of primordial wisdom."

"All follow after this very one" refers to the Bodhisattvas, who possess the vajra-body. "Of the mass of gnosis" refers to the nature of the Saṃbhogakāya. "As long as it arises from the place of birth."
With the three realms as a delightful path,
by means of the supreme application of Mahāmudrā,
all of those should be consumed.

"Born from a womb" refers to those born from a placenta (*jarāyuja*), from an egg (*aṇḍaja*), from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), or by spontaneous generation (*aupapāduka*). "By means of the application of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*)" means by way of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "One should enjoy" means by way of the unsurpassed teaching of the Dharma. "The Vajra-holders performed the exclamation" means that they uttered the words "Excellent! Excellent!"—this is the intended meaning. Thus spoke the Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas.
Having heard these vajra words,
he became joyful and delighted,
and was endowed with the activity of the Vajra of Speech.
The Great Mother Nairātmyā,
Vajra-Vairocana Īśvara,
and the Great King Vajrasattva;
The Great Sage, Supreme in Truth,
Vajrasūrya of Great Splendor,
And the Great Lord Hayagrīva—
And also as the very Body, Speech, and Mind; the body’s joints begin to move. *kāyavākcittam eva ceti* | *kāyavākcittam api* |
In a single moment, the Teacher, the King,
performed this directly before their eyes.
Then, the King Vajradhara, the Great Vajradhara of the Supreme Three Bodies, abiding in the samādhi of the Vajra of Equality, spoke these words:

"Abiding in the Mahāvajra-samādhi" means that Hevajra—who has ascended to the level of realization—is the Mahāvajra; the *samādhi* is the one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) having him as its object. "Abiding in that" is the meaning.
Having entered the Mother’s mandala, the eight-faced [one] is Mahābala.
He possesses sixteen hands,
with a radiance like that of a blue sapphire,
and great majesty, together with four feet.
Possessing a form that is both majestic and wrathful,
he abides in the dance posture of the half-lotus,
fully adorned with ornaments of bone.
The first face is black,
adorned with white and red;
the remaining faces are like bees.
The four māras are brought into equipoise; at the crown of the head is the supreme Vajra-holder; there, the vajra is black in color.
One should also meditate on the Great Light Rays;
at the very site of empowerment,
one is adorned by the five Buddhas.
An elephant, a horse, a donkey,
a female ox, a human, a śarabha,
and a cat— in these eight [skulls] on the right,
One should know the sequence beginning with the short *ga* and so forth;
[these correspond to] earth, water, wind, heat,
the moon, and the sun itself.
Yama and Vaiśravaṇa themselves are upon the eight skulls on the left;
this is the samādhi called "The Vajra of the Steadfast Great Being."
Apply GTI MUG to the vajra eye;
ZHE SDANG to the vajra ear;
likewise, SER, SNA, and 'DOD CHAGS [to the remaining senses].
One should meditate on emptiness and selflessness; she has one face and two arms,
and her various forms are the queens themselves.
"Holding a curved knife in the hand and bound by a skull-cup, their life-force abides perfectly above.

Regarding the phrase "the women indeed have various forms": therein, Mohavajrā is white; Dveṣavajrā is blue; Piśunavajrā is yellow; Rāgavajrā is red; Īrṣyāvajrā is green; and Nairātmyayoginī is blue. Regarding the phrase "their life-force abides perfectly above": they stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a sun-maṇḍala on top of corpses.
The Sky-Walker (Khecarī) herself, and likewise the One Who Dwells Beneath the Feet— by means of the ritual of these very [deities],...

"One should meditate on them as abiding in the three places" means by this very method: by way of having the sun as their seat and the sun as their radiance. Among them, Bhūcarī is red at the throat; Khecarī is black at the heart; and Pātālavāsinī is white in the body.
Oṃ, Great King of Action!
Adorned with the vajra of the syllable *yaṃ*,
great king of the mind-vajra,
you abide in the state of Vajrasattva.

He states their seed-syllables with the words beginning "Oṃkāra": Oṃkāra is that of Pātālavāsinī; Cittavajra, the syllable Hūṃ, is that of Khecarī. [The verse continues: "That supreme reality is speech; the path of speech is expressed as the manifest."
From the vajra of body and speech,
the phenomena arise as the three families;
*Āḥ* is the syllable of the *bhūcarī*s.
In the center of the sun mandala,
one should visualize a white female form holding a hook with the threatening gesture.
“White-complexioned with great light” means she is white in form;
this is the samādhi called “The White One Possessing the Vajra.”
In the center of the red mandala,
one should meditate on the form of Caṇḍālī;
she is fierce and has a complexion like the color of gold.
Vajrarāga, the Great Weapon;
dwelling in the center of the vajra mandala,
the vetālī is like blood.
Vajra-Chain, who acts with pride,
the female who binds one to enlightenment,
dwelling in the center of a mandala of light.
Then one should meditate on Ghasmarī; her hands are joined with a vajra and bell,
resembling a mārgad and an utpala.
"Vajra," and so forth. The meaning is that it is the yoga of the gatekeepers of Heruka, the Vajra. This is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "The Vajra Protectress" and "The Vajra Captor.
Regarding the four goddesses at the intermediate directions:
One should meditate through whatever application is appropriate: the Bodhicitta, the *Kāraṇḍavyūha* Sūtra,
and the great fire-pit of the Victor.

"One should meditate on the goddesses in the corners" means that the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, are to be visualized in the corners. The four items, such as the bell of bodhicitta, are their respective symbols in due order.
Thus, the non-dual yogi together with the outer [consort] should meditate on the Lord in that manner.
"Through the attachment of great passion,
one attains bliss free from the waves of the winds;
this is the samādhi called the Vajra of the Four Elements."

"Consisting of the vajra of the four elements," and so forth. In that context, the meaning is as follows: the vessel of bodhicitta is the water element; Mount Meru is the earth element; the fire pit is the fire element; and the great banner is the wind element. Alternatively, the intention is that these four, Pukkasī and the others, have the nature of earth and the other elements, and this is their meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Then, the Vajradhara King, the teacher of all the commitments of the three vehicles, abiding in the meditative absorption of all forms, uttered this melodic sound:

"Abiding in the samādhi of all forms" means that all the forms of the wrathful deities—such as their arms and so forth—are "all forms"; he abides therein with a mind one-pointed in samādhi. "This sound" refers to the speech consisting of mantra which is about to be described. The wrathful deity born from the syllable *Hūṃ* is always possessed of hatred.
If it does not succeed internally,
one should accomplish it through intense mental exertion:
*namaḥ samantabuddhebhyo namo vajramudgarahastvāya tsantamaṇḍalākṣepākarāya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then, by the mere explanation of this Great Wrathful One here, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas become terrified and tremble, and they call to mind the Lord Maheśvara,
the Vajra-holder. He is born from a lotus, free from attachment, with one or two arms.
"By the excellent application of the four *rig ma*s, may all the Buddhas completely fill [the space].

Regarding the passage beginning with "of women" (*nārīṇām*): having taken an auspicious skull-cup, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp upon its back using saffron, *gorocanā*, and the blood from the ring fingers. Having written the image of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the pericarp, and within that heart, the *mālā-mantra* ending with "summon such-and-such a woman" (*amukīm ākarṣaya jaḥ*), one should conceive of oneself in the form of Yamāri-Vajra. Then, by means of the practice of summoning and so forth performed with the four goddesses, Gaurī and the others, one brings all the Buddhas in the forms of Hevajra and so on.

The collective meaning is as follows: having filled [the space] up to every atom, one should step upon the heart of the image drawn on the skull-cup with the soles of the feet marked by vajra-hooks born from the *hūṃ* situated within a solar disc; then, for the summoning of a maiden, one should stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, and for the summoning of a man, in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and recite that Yamāri mantra together with the incitation.
"By means of the application of the dust of the footprints, one should step upon and pierce [him]."
"By means of the meditation on the generation of the three *skus*, one should summon the great maiden.

This states the second application, beginning with the words "foot," and so forth. "Foot-dust" (*pādapāṃśu*) refers to the dust from the feet of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). Its "preparation" (*vidhāna*) consists of making an image of the *sādhya* together with earth from both banks of a river. Then, having inserted the mantra written on birch bark or similar material into its heart, one should step upon it as before with the foot and recite that mantra.
