Regarding the words "three bodies" (*trikāya*), and so forth: the meaning is that [one performs] the meditation on the generation [of the deity] through the transformation of the emblem and seed-syllable of Yamāri, who is the embodiment of the three bodies.
This is the samādhi called Vajrayamāntaka.
Namaḥ samantabuddhebhyaḥ. Mahādaṇḍadhara vighnavidhvaṃsana surāmardana bhūtaniṣūdana hūṃ phaṭ.
Then, by explaining the great power of the Great Wrathful One, Aparājita, the bodhisattvas and others were made to tremble and were brought to mind.
For the spirits of the elemental classes,
the *piśācas*, and for the *ḍākinīs* and *kinnaras* who have been seized,
one should subdue them with the syllable *hūṃ* and seal them with the mudrā.
"Bliss itself through the pressing of the vajra" (*vajrapīḍanataḥ sukham eva*) means:
"seized" (*mudritām iti*) refers to those who have been grasped;

"the majesty of the utterance of *hūṃ*" (*hūṃkṛtāṭopa*) means that one, being personally engaged in the yoga of Aparājita, utters the mantra accompanied by the syllable *hūṃ*; "by the pressing of the vajra" (*vajrapīḍanataḥ*) means the pressing with the two vajras produced from the *hūṃ* seen in both hands together with their rays, or the striking with mustard seeds transformed into blazing vajras by means of the syllable *hūṃ*; from that, there is bliss, which is well-being (*svāsthya*).
The samādhi called "Invincible Vajra.
Namah samanta buddhebhyaḥ. Oṃ hulu hulu mahāpadma ākarṣaya mahāpiśācān āḥ.
Great poisons shall be summoned; likewise, those who are fainting shall be aroused.

"Draws [it] forth," and so on: having taken oneself as the support in the form of Padmāntaka, and seeing oneself seated upon the sun on the back of Garuḍa, one draws forth the poison located throughout the three worlds by means of the rays of the syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the sun at one's own heart while reciting the mantra. "The awakening of one who is asleep is likewise": having visualized oneself as before, one should see the poison residing in the body of the subject being driven outward from the head down to the soles of the feet by those rays, turning black.
This is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "The Vajra that Seizes the Lotus."
*Namaḥ samantabuddhebhyaḥ, namo vajrakrodhāya mahādāṃṣṭrotkaṭabhārāya, vajrasandohadarppāya, oṃ āmṛta kuṇḍali hūṃ phaṭ.* Then,
as the wrathful one who subdues obstructors spoke these vajra words, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas became displeased.

Having taken up dust from the footprint of one who has been carried away by the wind, and having grasped the name-card of the person to be accomplished, one should place it beneath the feet of the Gaṇapati while reciting "HŪṂ PHAṬ. By means of the pride of HŪṂ and the application of the wrathful mantra born from the *vajrāmṛta-samādhi*, even the Buddhas will be cast down.

"Stirred by the wind," and so forth. The meaning is that one should write the purpose at the end of the line, [beginning with] "on the sole of Gaṇapati's foot" and "the Kuṇḍalī. Here is the collective meaning: having drawn a great sword-wheel in the center of a large navel situated within a wind-circle—upon cloth lifted by a whirlwind or similar means—using a pen made from the wing of a large crow, with a liquid consisting of charcoal from wood burnt in a cemetery, yellow orpiment, poison, and *ariṣṭa* leaves, mixed with blood from the ring finger of the left foot; then, in its navel, [one draws] the effigy.

Having written that *mālā-mantra*—interwoven with the victim’s name and preceded by the *saṃcodana*—upon its heart, one should fashion an image using clay from a *kulāla* wheel, clay from a crossroads, and dust from a tree to be targeted, and place it within that heart. Then, having placed it in a skull-casket and performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), the practitioner himself, as a yogin of Vighnāntaka, should conceal the yantra—consecrated eight hundred times with the mantra beginning "Homage to all Buddhas" (*namaḥ samantabuddhebhyah*)—either in a mother’s house, a cremation ground, or at a crossroads.

And meditating upon the person to be accomplished as mounted on the back of a camel situated upon a circle of wind, being led toward the southern direction by a man holding a staff in his hand, one certainly effects their eradication.
This is the samādhi called "Vajra Nectar.
This activity should be thoroughly exhorted with the utmost secrecy.
This is called the "Vajra of Gnosis";
it will be accomplished in seven days.

"Prescribed by the ritual of application" means as follows: one who possesses the yoga of the Noble Nīladaṇḍa should fashion an image using charcoal from a funeral pyre, anthill earth, husks, parched grain, human flesh, and dust from the feet. Having written the *mālāmantra*—interspersed with the name of the target—upon a cloth from a cemetery using a pen made of human bone, with ink consisting of the juices of poison, blood, indigo, *trikuṭā*, *kāriṣṭa*, and leaves, in the center of a fire-maṇḍala marked with a double-vajra, he should insert it into the heart of the image, invoke [the deity], place it between two skull-caps, and then [of that]...

Enraged for the purpose of killing, one should step upon a stone, a bone, or a neem leaf with the left foot and recite the mantra accompanied by the command, "Kill so-and-so at midday or at midnight! HŪṂ PHAṬ! with wrathful speech; within seven days, he causes death.
NAMAḤ SAMANTABUDDHEBHYAḤ | OṂ YAMA-DAṆḌĀYA NĪLĀYA NĪLADAṆṬĀYA TURA TURA MURA MURA SARVADUṢṬĀNĀM ĀRAYA MĀRAYA HŪṂ PHAṬ ||

Then, by the teaching of the Great Wrathful One, the Blue Staffed Great Being, all sentient beings and the Buddhas were brought to doubt regarding their very lives. By merely reciting [the mantra] eight hundred times, through the rite of incitement for intense meditation, all malevolent ones will be bound.
This is the samādhi called the Vajra Pressed by the Armlet.

*Namaḥ samantabuddhebhyaḥ, namo mahābalāya, oṃ tśūṣma-krodharāja ā sarvanāgānāṃ hrīdayaṃ tāḍaya hūṃ phaṭ.* Then, by the explanation of the Great Fierce One (*Mahācaṇḍa*), the faces of the poisons are terrified and deprived of their power; they become frightened and tremble, and the Great Powerful One is brought to mind.

Regarding the eight *viṣyās*—the eight *nāgas* previously mentioned—one who possesses the yoga of the eight arms, four faces, and great strength should write, upon a baked clay dish (*pakvaśarāva*), with indigo juice, the mantra: "Oṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ, O Trident-bearer (*śūlapāṇi*), cause [the rain] to fall quickly! This should be written in the center of an eight-spoked wheel and discus, within an eight-petaled lotus. Having enclosed this with another dish (*śarāva*) to form a casket, wrapped it with blue thread, and having invoked Śūlinī and the *nāgas* with the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), worshipped them, and given the command, [one should place] the casket of the two dishes...
One should cast [the substance] into a lotus pond or similar site presided over by a nāga, preceded by the recitation of the mantra; then the nāgas will certainly send rain.
This is the samādhi called "Vajrabala Avalokiteśvara.
Namaḥ samantabuddhebhyo, namo ācala-kāmce-tatte, motta motta, tutta tutta, gha gha, ghātaya ghātaya hūṃ phaṭ.
Then, as the great wrathful Acala was proclaimed by the Great Being, the gods, nāgas, and great yakṣas fainted and fell to the ground.
"Now, by means of this ritual of the Lion-Rider, the King of Wrathful Deities,
through the yoga of the Vajra Mandala,"
"Men and gods are summoned.

Regarding "mounted on a lion," and so forth: the yogin, possessing the yoga of the immovable wrathful deity, should visualize the object of practice—being drawn by a deity who is mounted upon a wind-maṇḍala born from the syllable *yaṃ* and seated upon a lion born from the syllable *siṃ*, and who holds a noose and a goad—in such a way that he has fallen at his feet; thus he summons him.
*Oṃ sumbha ni sumbha hūṃ, gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ, gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ, ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ phaṭ.*
By the laughter of the great wrathful one, Vajrapātālavāsī, together with the asura maiden Gaurī,
[the earth] was shaken.
Not appearing for even a moment,
they are firmly bound by the vajra noose;
having been torn apart by the iron hook—
"By means of meditating on the body, speech, and mind, one should summon all maidens;
thus, 'one should summon all maidens' [is said]. By the very same previous sequence, in the yoga of the deity, there is yet another distinction."
This is the samādhi called "Summoning the Three Worlds.
Vajradharma is the great rain-cloud; Vajrasattva is the supreme rain.
The great assembly of Vajrasūrya,
the vast multitude of supreme steeds, and the clouds of benefit— these are the rain-clouds.
If even the Buddhas are summoned by the meditation of the "Vajra Hook of Subduing," what need is there to mention ordinary beings?
Visualize one's own consort as a noble being,
adorned with the three bodies and vajra ornaments;
through the application of the hook and so forth, [the union is accomplished].
"One should summon the woman and eat her.

This refers to the "personification of ignorance" (*avidyāpuruṣa*). Having visualized any one of the five *ḍākas* together with his consort, [one acts] "by means of the application of the hook and so forth," that is, by means of Gaurī holding a noose and a hook emerging from the seed-syllable in the heart. "The maiden" refers to her mounted upon the wind-maṇḍala. "By the application of the vajra-hook" means having formed it in the shape of a hook. Then the Blessed One proclaimed the samaya for summoning with the great vajra.
NAMAḤ SAMANTABUDDHEBHYAḤ, OṂ TĀKKI HŪṂ JAḤ!
And also,
through the application of the vajra hook, [one should] summon and purify.
At the time when the moon is waxing,
one should perform the practice after having placed [the image] upon a donkey; even by merely writing down the name, [the goal will be attained].
By reciting one hundred times clearly,
one shall summon the fierce Indras, together with their minor attendants, who possess speech and have no fixed abode.
This is the samādhi called “The Iron Hook of the Vow.
Abiding in meditative concentration, mantra, and samādhi,
one’s own consort is the personified self.
"He should be held at the place of summoning;
the Sage does not change otherwise.
By stating "he holds the station of summoning," he explains summoning by way of another method.
The meaning is that this has already been explained immediately [prior], and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

Namaḥ samanta-buddhānām | Namaḥ samanta-dharmāṇām | Namaḥ samanta-saṃghānām | Oṃ sītātapatre | Oṃ bimale | Oṃ śaṅkare | Oṃ praty-aṅgīre | Oṃ vajra-auṣṇīṣa-tsakra-varti-sarvayantra-mantra-mūla-karma-yantra-nīta-dāna-kīlanāṃ bāma-ma-kṛtāṃ yānaka-na-citta-kṛtāṃ tattata sarba ndu tstshinda ||
TSITSAṂDA, BHINDA BHINDA, TSIRI TSIRI, GIRI GIRI, MARA MARA, HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ PHAṬ.
For the application of self-protection, and for the destruction of the applications of the Tantras and so forth.

"Having prepared the *vidyā* for the arm" means that one should draw an eight-spoked wheel on birch bark or similar material; having written *Sumbha* and *Nisumbha* in the center, the mantra of the White Parasol (*Sitātapatra*) along the rim of the wheel, and the mantras of the eight wrathful deities (*krodha*) on the spokes in their respective places, one should fashion this *vidyā* and wear it on the arm or the neck.
This is the samādhi called "The Great Wrathful One,
Wheel-Vajra. Even in a secluded forest grove,
one should completely abandon all doubt.
If one accomplishes this supreme yoga,
one will not become anything other than a Sage.
This is the fourth chapter, titled "The Vajra Entrance into the Mantra of the Great Wrathful One’s Wheel."
The Fourth Chapter. || O ||
"Then the Blessed One, the Holder of the Vajra,
entered the hearts of all sentient beings;
he is born from omniscient primordial wisdom."
"Perfectly and thoroughly distinguished," *sārvajñam* means "pertaining to the omniscient one.
"Having clearly meditated on the form of the Buddha,"
One should meditate intensely on Vajrasattva;
having meditated intensely on the image of the Buddha,
one should bring to mind Vairocana.

"The image of the Buddha" refers to Vajrasattva, who is perfected through the sequence of the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*). "Vajrasattva" refers to Śrī Heruka. This should be understood in other instances as well. "Having clearly visualized the image of the Buddha, one should clearly visualize Vajrasūrya."
Having meditated on the image of the Buddha,
one should meditate on Vajrarāga; having meditated on the images of the Buddhas, [one should meditate on Vajrarāga].
One should thoroughly meditate on the reality that possesses meaning;
one should constantly meditate on the mandalas arising from the images of the Buddhas.
"Maṇḍalas arisen from the images of the Buddhas" means the deities of the maṇḍala who have arisen from the Vajradhara of the fivefold causes.
With this mantra of all [the deities],
one should place [them] in the heart, the abode of gnosis.
By thoroughly applying oneself to the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*), one will attain the awakening of a Buddha.

Regarding "of the mantras": this refers to the mantra-deities. Regarding "the state of wisdom": this refers to the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*). "Marked with signs and seed-syllables" means equal to oneself. "By the application of the being and wisdom" means by entering the commitment-maṇḍala (*samayamaṇḍala*) of the wisdom-being. "The awakening of a Buddha" means one should contemplate the unity of the two, like milk and water.
When the letters of the mantra have been completed,
one should examine the mudrās and the hand gestures;
having performed the emanation and reabsorption, [one should proceed].
Having understood the threefold nature of the sounds that constitute the very arising of the mandalas,
one should offer them to the deities.

"By one's own mantra," and so forth. The meaning is that one should visualize the signs, such as the vajra, through the transformation of their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), and having performed the emanation and reabsorption [of light], the arising of the deities should be contemplated. "The sound," and so forth. It is threefold, distinguished as superior, inferior, and middling. "Having recognized the three types of form, one should offer them to the deities. [This refers to] the Blessed One Vajradhara, the Great Renowned Vajrasattva.
That very Blessed King is the Lord Vajra-Vairocana;
having recognized the three types of fragrance, one should offer them to the deities.
That very Blessed Buddha is renowned as Ratnakūṭa.
Having discerned the three types of taste, one should offer them to the deities;
that very [taste] is the Blessed One Desire itself, the Tathāgata Vajradharma.
Having discerned the three types of touch, one should offer them to the deities.

One should meditate on the five mandalas that summarize the protective samaya, which are the Blessed One Viśvarūpa, the bestower of meaningful fruit. "Situated in the midst of the protective samaya" means being within the protective wheel. "The five mandalas" refers to the mandala of withdrawal, which consists of the nature of the five mandalas.

"Five-fifths-nature Perfect Buddha," and so forth. The meaning is that Śrī Heruka and the others each possess a fivefold nature by virtue of having the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), as their essential nature; they are endowed with the five qualities and desire to fully cultivate the five wisdoms, pervaded by all various rays of light.
From the various [tantras], it is described as an activity;
the mandala that summarizes everything should be drawn with colored powders by means of the twenty-fivefold division.

"Even in the case of *rajas*"—by the word "even," it is implied that this also applies to the *sūtra*. In that regard, there are twenty-five divisions: for Śāśvata, they are blue, yellow, red, green, and white; for Sūrya, white, blue, red, green, and yellow; for Narteśvara, white, yellow, blue, green, and red; for Aśva, white, yellow, red, blue, and green; and for Hevajra, white, yellow, red, green, and blue, proceeding in a clockwise direction. This is the intended meaning according to the rule for the inner region. By the nature of the five Buddhas, They are renowned as the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The mandala of the Buddha Lord is renowned in the eastern quarter;
in the south is that of Vajrasūrya; in the west, that of Rāgavajra;
in the north, that of Aśvarāja; and in the center, that of Vajrasattva.
In the east is great white, and the south is correctly endowed with yellow;
red is on the western side, and vermilion is correctly placed in the north.
In all the intermediate directions, as well as on the surfaces of the doors and the upper porticos, [the colors are likewise arranged].
Adorned with vajras and jewels, beautified by various manifestations,
that which constitutes the center of the maṇḍala of whichever Buddha Lord it may be is called his very maṇḍala; it is the maṇḍala that fully upholds the essence.

"Of whichever [deity]," and so forth. The meaning is that for whichever [deity], such as Hevajra, there is a maṇḍala within the center of the *saṃhāramaṇḍala*, that very one holds the status of the leader (*nāyaka*) therein. Whether one meditates on each individual maṇḍala, or else the *saṃhāramaṇḍala*, with eight [deities] residing in the center, or else twenty-five.

Alternatively, "the maṇḍala of withdrawal" refers to the fifth maṇḍala situated in the center of the great maṇḍala. Regarding the phrase "situated in the middle of the eight-eights": that which contains eight times eight squares is the "eight-eights"; and since it is both the eight-eights and the center with respect to the great maṇḍala, it is the "middle of the eight-eights. That which stands in that form is "situated in the middle of the eight-eights. Furthermore, regarding "in twenty-five": it is characterized by twenty-five powders (*rajas*).

At the entrance of the condensed maṇḍala, one should assign the Hook, the Noose, likewise the Chain, and the Vajra as the gatekeepers of the entrance (*dvārapālān*); that is, the female gatekeepers (*dvārapālīḥ*). The term "Hook" (*aṅkuśam*) refers to the goddess Aṅkuśī; the same applies elsewhere as well.
The Blessed One spoke this great samaya of condensation:
"An elephant, a vulture, likewise a rhinoceros, a musk deer,
and a tiger, a monkey, and a short-nosed ox— these are on the right of Vajradharma."
The lion that drinks the flowing water, likewise the elephant dwelling in the lake,
the deer, and the boar— these always abide on the left side;
as do the peacock, the buffalo, the makara, the sun-king, and the crocodile.
Equal to the wind of the *og gi* [lower] region, and on the right side of the rabbit’s benefit,
there is *mīnarāja*, and also *rohita*.
There is the great frog, the cloud-velocity, the mouth-water, the eye-medicine, and the *byi la* [mouse] which resembles them.
G-yag and dri-ldan are explained as being likewise; they are on the eight left skulls.
Ka-raṇḍa and 'khor-lo, along with lug, tsa-ko-ra, bya-khra, hor-mo-'ol-ba, and ku-ra, are on the right side of the sun.
Stobs kyi rgyu (Śatabhiṣaj), Dung skyong (Pūrvabhadrapadā), the noble Padma (Padmapāṇi) and Pad bzang (Bhadrapada),
'Jog po (Revatī), Nor rgyas mtha' yas (Vāsuki)— these are on the left of Rin chen rgyal po (Ratnarāja).
Gza' lag (Budha), Phur bu (Śukra), Mjug ring (Rāhu), Sgra gcan (Ketu), Mig dmar pa (Maṅgala), and Pa sangs (Bṛhaspati);
Spendra, Vyāpin, and Aśvapati are renowned as being on the right;
Indrā, Brahmā, and likewise Rudra, Kāmadeva, and Kapālin,
along with Nagna and Vāsuki, and the one called Balin, are on the left.
Swelling, gas, as well as consumption, leprosy, gout, and jaundice;
the nature of abdominal dropsy and urinary disorders is also well known in elephants and other [animals].
Furthermore, there are *lcat-stegs*, *rjed-byed*, *khrag-rdog*, *cod-nad*, and *rgyal-po*.
Scrofula, abdominal tumors, and wasting diseases; jaundice, leprosy, and so forth; ringworm, dental ailments, and likewise bile, blood, and wind disorders;
phlegm, seminal leakage, emaciation, and skin diseases such as herpes and scabies.
Lameness, ailments of the calves, rheumatism, enlargement of the intestines, and flatulence;
fever, dysentery, and hemorrhoids—these are well known as *karanda* and so forth.
Likewise, wind-disorders, indigestion, obscurations, demonic possession, cataracts, and exhaustion.
[The planets] are Śukra (Venus), Ketu, Mars, Rāhu, Jupiter, Mercury, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "among the migrations, the human is supreme" and so on: among the five migrations (*gati*), the human migration is the most excellent, because it is precisely therein that the three types of awakening are attained—this is the intended meaning. "And she" refers to those diseases such as the elephant-disease (*gajaroga*) and so forth. "She ran" refers to the diseases situated in the right skull-hemisphere; "those situated in the left skull-hemisphere" refers to the medicines—the sense being that [she ran] for the sake of all of them.
Seeing that all [beings] are pervaded by disease, I shall place within my own body the Buddha renowned as "The Radiant. Without causing distress to sentient beings,
the Buddha assumes the illnesses of elephants and other creatures in order to pacify their diseases.
When one has meditated in this way: there is no illness, no aging, and no exhaustion;
there is no death and no certainty of passing away; there is no pride and no delusion;
there is no hunger and no meditative cultivation; and likewise, there is no suffering or miserable rebirths.
Neither by gods, nor by asuras, nor by humans, nor by anyone else whatsoever is illness caused.
This is the fifth chapter, titled "The Emission of Breath that Completely Pacifies All Illnesses.
|| Pañcamaḥ paṭalaḥ || o ||
Then the King Vajradhara, the Sustainer of All Bodies, who captivates the minds of the ḍākinīs, spoke these words:
"Focusing on the recollection of the mind, one should meditate on the recollection of the Buddha;
having contemplated the jewel of the mind, one should meditate on the recollection of the Dharma."

The meaning of "recollection of mind" (*cittānusmṛti*) and so forth is that, at the time of emanation for the sake of sentient beings, one should perform the recollection of Hevajra and others through the sequence of radiating and withdrawing. "The jewel of mind" refers to Ratnasambhava, who is inseparable from the mind. Through the yoga of the recollection of mind, One should thoroughly meditate upon the Great Wheel; This yoga is the supreme excellence, Which has neither arisen nor will ever arise.
"Great Wheel" refers to the mandala of reabsorption. Having visualized Vajrasattva, one should seal with the four mudrās;
having visualized Vairocana, one should seal by means of the visualization of the mudrās.

"Vajrasattva" refers to Hevajra. "By means of the four mudrās" refers to the four wheels, beginning with the *nirmāṇa*-cakra. The same applies to Śāśvata and the others as well. Through the application of the vajra-mudrā, one should clearly meditate on the heap of jewels; through the excellent application of the dharma-mudrā, one should seal with the karma-vajra-mudrā.
"King of Hatred, Great King, who brings all defects to an end;
one should meditate on [him] as emanating and reabsorbing; the reabsorption is also correctly explained.
With the passage beginning with "King of Hatred" and ending with "one should visualize," the instruction on the recollections (*anusmṛti*) has been stated.

"By means of the yoga of radiation" means that one should likewise instruct on the withdrawal [of the visualization] through the cloud-like emanation of the mantra-bindu from one's own body, or through the cloud of symbols. In that very same [text]: "When meditating intensely upon the Buddha-protector, pervaded by clouds of Buddhas, one should meditate intensely upon the awakening of the Buddhas through the yoga of radiation and withdrawal."
The great jewel of the mind completely eliminates the faults of Māra;
by means of the mental rain-cloud formation, the withdrawal shall once again be demonstrated.
Regarding "the syllable of the mind" (*cittākṣaram*): it is the seed-syllable of Hevajra. Thus, elsewhere as well, by the word "syllable," only the seed-syllable is intended.
The Dharma King, Great Delusion, who possesses a form that expands and contracts—
by meditating upon him as empowered during the four sessions, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
Contemplating the mind as being like a swift traveler, one offers the fruit of the immeasurable.
One should also meditate on the gathering by means of the great cloud of rain from the supreme *ṛta*.
Thus the Blessed One spoke these words regarding the great samaya of expansion and gathering:
"Abiding in the center of the solar mandala, one should meditate on the forms of the mind."
Abiding in the center of the stainless maṇḍala, one should clearly visualize the syllables of the Body. Abiding in the center of the blood maṇḍala, one should place the precious syllable of Mind.
In the center of the wheel of Dharma, one should visualize the syllables of speech. The red maṇḍala is the sun maṇḍala; the dharma maṇḍala is the sun maṇḍala.
In the center of the activity maṇḍala, there exists the form of that very syllable.
"One who does not perform the three *skus* (bodies) should meditate on Jñānavajra.

This refers to the *karmamaṇḍala*, the solar maṇḍala, which is "indestructible," and so forth. The sequence is that one should understand that the symbols, such as the vajra, are to be placed upon the heads of Hevajra and the others within the maṇḍala to be meditated upon. "The indestructible Vajrasattva [is] the Dharmacakra of Vairocana."

The precious jewel of the awakened mind, the lotus of excellence with its crimson petals, and the meaningful sword of wisdom— through the very nature of this sharp wisdom, once the mountain of conceptual thought has been severed, one will become possessed of Mahāmudrā.
In the hundred million *Dpag bsam* (Kalpadruma) [tantras], one should meditate upon the vajra mandala;
likewise, the mandala of benefit itself, the great light of the heap of jewels,
extending for ten million *yojanas*, is thus immeasurable.

In the center of the expanse of space, one should meditate on the wisdom maṇḍala, adorned with clouds of buddhas, blazing with great rays of various light, and arising from the Great Lord Dharmaskandha and the Tathāgata Vajrakarma.
"Filled with the five qualities of desire, appearing in various forms everywhere, one should worship with all offerings.
[This refers to the phrase] "situated in the center of the space-element": having summoned [the deity] from the seed-syllable in the heart, one establishes it in the space before oneself.
"By means of the yoga of the goddesses of the corners (koṇadevī), one should thoroughly accomplish the ocean of primordial wisdom (jñāna).
The great blazing Vajra of Wisdom is placed within the maṇḍala of the commitment (samaya).

Regarding "by means of the yoga of the goddesses of the corners": because they are metaphorically designated as "goddesses of the corners" due to their proximity to the corners, [it refers to] the goddesses such as Gaurī and the others, through the ritual procedures of summoning and so forth.
The yogi, equal to all Buddhas, becomes non-dual in an instant; this is the unification with the maṇḍala of the pledge (samayamaṇḍala).
[One should offer] the *ru-rakṣa* and the conch-shell horn, the meat of the cow, and the *bad-’bras* fruit.
One endowed with meditative concentration should perform mantra recitation using coral and the like, as well as conch shells and the like.
In order to bring the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, ḍākinīs, and one’s own consort into direct presence,
one should utter the mantra while calling for their attention.

Just as when some great being becomes enraged for a moment, [others] come upon merely hearing of it, so too does the Buddha arrive in a single instant. "The arrival of the Buddha" (*buddhāgama*) means the coming of the Buddha.
"By means of a pretext" (*cchalenaiva*) means "remaining under the guise of [something else]"; this is the ellipsis. For this very reason, he says "he too," and so forth:
"In thousands of world-systems, within the sky-dwellings of the realm of space, the Buddhas—equal to space—dwell in the state of bliss of Mahāmudrā."
The masters of the vidyā-mantras have departed; the Vajra-Eye beholds all.
Whoever attains the stages of mantra, oh, by that very person enlightenment is attained!
Even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas first undertake the conduct of mantra.
By the excellent application of the Vajra Mantra, one attains incomparable primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
The Buddha who knows in this way, abiding in the stages of mantra conduct, perceives the very fruit itself; that is described as the equality of the Buddhas.

"By taking pride in being a Buddha, one meditates upon the luminous realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); therefore, sentient beings become equal to Buddhas. The concise meaning is as follows: having focused on the pride of being a Buddha—that is, having resolved that oneself is the form of a Buddha—one meditates upon the dharmadhātu; because of that, [the practitioner] is indeed a Buddha.
Just as the world is awakened as the Buddha, and just as the Dharma is the Saṅgha,
so too is the realm of sentient beings explained. Stainless like space,
the precious mind is made defiled by the conceptualizations of pure investigation.
Through the purity of the mind, one becomes pure; just as space is indestructible, so too is the mind like space.
By exhorting the jewel of the mind, the meditation on the nature of mind is itself buddhahood; thus, in this very birth, one is the sublime Buddha.

"Because of the impelling of the jewel of the mind" means because of the mind-jewel’s perception of things as they truly are. "There is no Buddha and no person apart from the precious mind; there is not the slightest external thing that is the object of the locus of consciousness."
"By means of the mind alone, one attains the state of all Buddhas, the great sovereign of the three realms, the great king of the three worlds, through a single thought.
[The phrase "great sovereignty over the three realms" refers to the two bodies: the Enjoyment Body and the Emanation Body.]
Therefore, regarding the phrase "by the king of mantras," it should be understood that "mantra" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), and thus [the phrase] also implies "by the deities."
Form, sound, and likewise smell, Taste, and the nature of the tangible— The dharmadhātu is supremely peaceful; This is proclaimed as the supreme jewel.
Form, feeling, perception, Volitional formations, and consciousness itself—

All these four hundred billion worlds arise from the mind; this Sage is not otherwise. Like a precious wish-fulfilling jewel that bestows the fruit of all desired aims, the reality of the mind is pure by nature and bestows the fruit of buddhahood and enlightenment.
For this very reason, by means of the Buddha’s exhortation of the vajra of the mind,
he bestows the siddhi of *ardhaprīti* (half-delight) characterized by that profound aspect. This is the sixth chapter,
the Illumination of the Essence of Vajrasattva.
The Sixth Chapter. || O ||
Then, the Great Vajra Holder, the Possessor of the Vajra, abiding in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the yoga that generates the *guhya* (mandala) of the ḍākinīs, spoke this yoga of himself:

"Vajra" means that because its intrinsic nature is the *dharmakāya*, it is equal to a vajra. "Abiding in the meditative absorption of the arising of yoga": yoga is the yoga of the deity; its arising is the generation [of that deity]. Within that, "meditative absorption" is one-pointedness. "Abiding therein" means remaining in that state. "The yoga of oneself" refers to the practitioner’s own yoga with the deity.
The Buddha’s abode is perfectly complete; through the meditation on the five aspects, the nature of Samantabhadra, and the accomplishment of one's own supreme deity, [one attains it].

Regarding the phrase "in the accomplishment of the Buddha-abode": this refers to the accomplishment of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). The meaning is the meditation on the fivefold visualization of the form within each maṇḍala—namely, the meditation on the radiation and reabsorption of the moon, sun, seed-syllables, and emblems, as well as the generation of the deities. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "the true nature (*sadbhāva*) of Samantabhadra. This means the accomplishment of the Causal Vajradhara within each maṇḍala. Furthermore, the practice of one's own tutelary deity (*svādhidaivata-sādhana*) serves as the individual cause for the accomplishment of the leaders and the retinue deities within each maṇḍala. [This includes] the arrangement of the various maṇḍalas, the offerings, praises, nectar-offerings (*amṛta*), and so forth.

One should meditate on it following the *rim pa* (sequence/stages); this is held to be the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). For this very reason, it says: "The arrangement (*nyāsa*) of the maṇḍalas in that manner.
*Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
Showing the six limbs, he says: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka* and so forth. The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, spoke these words: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatāmṛtasvādavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitāyus, spoke these words:
*Oṃ sarvatathāgatastutivajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ koṇyām*.
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, spoke these words.
Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrāśvaśreṣṭha:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ.
When the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrasūrya, had spoken thus, [he said]:
"The Great King Vairocana, whose body is both emanated and withdrawn,
who is born from the syllable of the dharmadhātu— he shall manifest the abode of the Buddhas."
Oṃ sarvatathāgatānīlaya vajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ.
This is the samādhi called Vairocana-vajra.
Abiding in the center of the expanse of space, the maṇḍala itself is the nature of the four elements.
Above that, one should visualize the Buddha; having emanated [light], one should arrange the celestial palace (*vimāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the maṇḍala whose nature consists of the four elements," this refers to the maṇḍalas of earth and so forth. "The Buddha above that" means: having meditated on Vairocana through the transformation of the syllable *BHRŪṂ* and the wheel, one should emanate and place the peaked palace (*kūṭāgāra*). According to the oral instruction, one should visualize the peaked palace by completely subduing all [other appearances].
Because it is indestructible like a vajra, one should therefore meditate on Akṣobhya.
From the *Recollection of the Arisen Ma*: "Vairocana is indeed the Benefactor (*hitatva*).
The passage beginning with "indestructible" (*abhedyam*) is easy to understand.
"The supreme among the supreme of jewels—this is explained as the jewel-like mind."
The Great King, the Vajradharma, from the one who holds the nature of passion, dwells in the state of Vajrasattva; thus the mind is explained as "passion.
Because that which is devoid of fruit is not accomplished, it is therefore renowned as "Amogha" (the Meaningful).
The samādhi called "The Beautiful Vidyā Vajrā.

Regarding the phrase *vidyāvacana* and so forth: *vidyās* are the five empowerments (*pañcābhiṣekas*). The meaning is that it is such because in this samādhi there is the vajra of their proclamation. "The first is the vase empowerment; the second is the secret empowerment."
Third is the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*). "Just as the body is the Tathāgata" refers to the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*);

"the master consecration" (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is that which is like it. "Just as it is not so" means that just as there is knowledge of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna*), the characterized object (*lakṣya*) does not exist [independently], because they are contrary [to one another]. Having drawn the excellent mandala, by means of the ritual for the melting of the samaya,
"Having generated the meditative concentration of *hām*, at that time one should give the breath.

‘One should draw the supreme mandala’ indicates the master’s initiation (*ācāryaseka*). ‘By means of the ritual of the seminal essence of the pledge (*samaya*)’ indicates the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*). ‘Having performed the fire offering or that which is born of meditation’ indicates the wisdom-knowledge initiation (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*). ‘Then one should release the exhalation’ indicates the fourth [initiation].
‘Possessing the five ḍākinīs and filled with the five pledges (*samaya*)...’"

"By means of the assembly of ḍākinīs, through the excellent application of the vajra-seed," and so forth—this verse indicates the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*). Regarding "through the application of the vajra-seed" and so on: having visualized oneself as the presiding deity (*adhipati*) arising from the melting of the bodhicitta of the samaya of all Tathāgatas, and having meditated upon the disciple in the form of Vairocana, one should confer the consecration; this is the remainder [of the meaning].
"Having made oneself the *adhidaiva* (superior deity), one should always contemplate the disciple."
By means of the name of the [Buddha] family in succession, the disciple is empowered as a Vajra-holder (*vajradhara*);
"dhāraya" means by means of the retention of the empowerment mantra, that is, by its recitation. "By the name of the family" means by a name corresponding to the family; this is the intended sense.
With the forms of Locanā, Śrī Herukī, Tārā, Pāṇḍarā, and so forth...

By means of the vajra consort’s thorough application, the unsurpassed vajra shall be explained. Now, he speaks of the indication of the secret empowerment with the words beginning with “Locanā” and so forth, and “the unsurpassed vajra” and so forth. The intended meaning is that the *bodhicitta* which arises through the sprinkling is the nature of the unsurpassed reality (*tattva*).
This unsurpassed reality is non-dual and without syllables.
The dharmadhātu is luminous clarity; it is the savoring of the taste of sublime bliss.
This very point is expressed by the words beginning with "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
It is the samādhi called "the vajra free from obscuration."
"Unobscured," and so forth. The meaning is: that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which the unobscured vajra—the purification of phenomena—is accomplished by way of being nectar.
"By the ritual procedure" means by way of accomplishing the state of being nectar.
*Ga dang ha* and so forth; first and last, endowed with *śva*.
"Exceedingly luminous and truly sublime, bestowing all siddhis—
partake of this vajra nectar of the assembly! By merely consuming these,
the yogin becomes equal to all Buddhas and identical to the Vajra."
"In the abode of vajra-amṛta" means having become the basis for liberation, which is of an indivisible nature through service; that is to say, having attained the state of being the cause.
"All afflictions are completely pacified; That is the majestic, great body, Captivating the minds of all the world, Victorious over all adversaries."
Adorned by the Lord of All Worlds, he is proclaimed as the leader of the gods;
he becomes the very essence of the five ḍākinīs. Profound is the fruit of the Dharma.
This is the samādhi called "The Vajra that Has Consumed the Great Samaya Resolve."
O yogin supported by Mi-bskyod-pa (Akṣobhya), may all illnesses be utterly dispelled!
May you always possess the great water-crystal [moon];
the great King Amogharāja, the undecaying Vajrasūrya, arises as the limb of vajra-life.
"Born from the limbs of a vajra-being" means that he desires flesh and acts according to his will.

Accomplishing the *don kun* (all aims) and possessing glory, one is thus called a yogin. Through the application of drinking the *mi bskyod pa* (Akṣobhya), one will live for five thousand [years]. The beneficial ground is said to be ten thousand; by the *rdo rje nyi ma* (Vajrasūrya), one hundred million; by the *tshe dpag med* (Amitāyus), immeasurable; and by the seven, it is explained as lasting as long as space. The *rdo rje nyi ma* and *dpag med* are the very root of the sādhanas for cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

"O Yogin, by meditating on this today, you will become like Samantabhadra. This wisdom of the perfection of insight is called the Vajra Sun. It is the abode of all phenomena, the Tathāgata Amitāyus. Mounted upon skillful means and wisdom, it pervades all the three realms—upon the earth, beneath the earth, and in the sky—with blood and semen."

The Lord of the Family, whose body pervades all, spoke this: "The nails and hair are likewise the *dhātus*; One should analyze the semen. In fat and blood there is great splendor; In marrow and bone is the Vajradhara. All are the Protector Vairocana; In the channels and flesh is the King of the Seven. Regarding these, the Vajraḍākinīs explain them as the five Buddhas. [On] the earth...

Bhūmā is completely pure; the eye is the beautiful wheel itself. The Vajra Lady is faith, and the Lotus Maiden is passion. Tārā is the complete purity of wind; she is the Vajra Lady of faith, known as the Vajra Ḍākinī. The Lord of the Pavilion commanded these.
This is the seventh chapter, titled "The Purity of All Mantras: The Emergence of the Supreme Five Nectars, the Vajra. || Seventh Chapter || o ||
"You who perfectly protect the Vajra of Hatred, whose mind and Dharma are utterly pure, and who have truly adorned the body of a deity—
Puṣyaśiri, look upon me swiftly! O Guide,
for the sake of the world, please abandon emptiness and accept birth!"
You who fully protect the vajra of delusion, the Lord of Form, adorned with the reflection of the Dharma-body,
O Protector Śrīparvata, look upon me swiftly!
For the sake of healing the world, O Guide, please abandon emptiness and accept birth.
You who fully protect the Vajra of Passion, through the correct discernment of your pure speech, you perfectly adorn the body of a deity;
O You who possess the supreme [wisdom], look swiftly upon me!
For the sake of the world’s physicians, the Guides, it is fitting for You to abandon emptiness and take birth.
O Protector of all Buddhas, who through the equality of all forms perfectly adorns the body of a deity— O Lord of Ḍombhī,
look upon me swiftly! O Guide,
for the sake of the world’s medicine, please abandon emptiness and accept birth.
The samādhi called "Vajra that Causes All to Accept.

Regarding *sarvakṛtya*: those for whom every task (*kṛtya*) has been accomplished are the "All-Accomplishers" (*sarvakṛtyas*), namely the Tathāgatas. The meaning is that this is the meditative absorption for the purpose of rousing them.
"By this, all those who possess the wheel shall be generated."
The Lord of the Mandala, possessing the Vajra of Wisdom, spoke thus: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatākṣarī vajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ.* *Oṃ sarvatathāgatabhūtsarī vajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ.*
Oṃ sarvatathāgatālāpasiṃhavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham.

With the mantra beginning “Oṃ sarvatathāgata,” he states the empowerment mantra for Khecarī and the others: "The empowerments of the qualities of body, speech, and mind shall always abide [within them]."
This should be performed by one possessing the Vajra of Gnosis; this is the teaching on the stages of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*).
"Body, speech, and mind," and so forth, is easy to understand. Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Lord of Body, Speech, and Mind.

"Through the application of Mahāmudrā, one should purify the jewel of the body; having meditated upon the Vajra of Dhyāna, one thoroughly accomplishes the jewel of the mind. Regarding "Mahāmudrā" and so forth: Mahāmudrā is the body of the deity; its application is the superimposition [of that form] upon one's own body. By means of that, one should purify the body through the Vajra of Dhyāna—the meditation on the form of the deity or something else by means of the mind. By that, [one purifies] the mind through mantra-recitation, and speech [is purified]; such is the intended meaning.
"By means of the excellence of vajra recitation, the vajra of speech becomes stainless.
Through the supreme application of the Vajra of Delusion, the eye-consciousness is joined.
The passage beginning with *mohavajra* is easy to understand.
With the thought of Vajra Hatred, one contemplates the gateway of sound;
with Se-vajra, the nose; with Rāga-vajra, the six flavors;
with Īrṣyā-vajra, the body; and with Samantabhadra, the mind.
O Nairātmyā, Lady of the Ḍākinīs, these [elements] are thoroughly purified;
even if there is no contradiction, at that time the reality of the Victor is purified.
Abiding correctly in the truth of the conventional, one meditates on the mere phenomena of the wheel-form.

"Even though," and so forth. "Contradictory" (*viruddha*) means that which is opposed. "Even though that [is so]" means "nevertheless. "Of the Victors" (*jinānām*) means "by the Victors. Why is this so? He says: "Conventional reality," and so forth. The "wheel" (*cakra*) is the maṇḍala-wheel. Just as it is according to conventional usage (*saṃdhyā-vyavahāra*), so too its purification is merely by way of convention. For "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*)—the sense is that through the nature of phenomena there is merely the dissolution of form and merely the self-awareness of its own essence; nothing else exists at all.

From the practice of the non-arising of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatāvastu*), all persons are utterly abandoned; the worldly cannot conceive of the world as a realm of transmigration, for by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all things are completely pure. From the perspective of ultimate truth, neither the object of apprehension nor the subject of apprehension exists.

"Due to the discernment of reality (*bhūtaviveka*)" means due to the thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of reality, which is empty of duality. He states this very point with the words "all," and so forth. Since the entire world is devoid of a person (*pudgala*) and so on, in the form of a grasper and so forth, therefore the course of the world—the cognition of things as they truly are—cannot be conceived by the foolish. Because it is thus, [he says] "by the forms of phenomena" (*dharmarūpaiḥ*), and so forth; the meaning is that everything is indeed pure by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). "The medicine for the body of those afflicted by the fever and poison of the ignorant is the very poison of others."

Just as water that has entered an ear, or alternatively, water itself becomes the very means [of its removal], he states the example with the words beginning "dagdhānām" (for those who are burned). Like poison—meaning a medicine that produces pustules and so forth—for one whose body is afflicted, that is, for one whose body is impaired; other poison refers directly to the verbal expression of the word "poison.
Just as minds agitated by wind, likewise the wise [handle] beans, peas, and lentils.
Even those deluded by attachment are tormented by the fire of desire; the worldly [beings] produced by desire are brought to exhaustion through the disparagement of desire.
By thoroughly knowing desire as a vajra, the mind becomes Vajrasattva.

"Exhaustion" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); the meaning is the manifest enlightenment of one free from passion (*vītarāgābhisaṃbodhi*). Regarding "through the thorough knowledge of vajra-passion": because passion is purified by means of the forms of the deities and so forth. As it is said: "By the attachment of passion, the world is said to be pervaded;
The manifest enlightenment of one free from passion is not desired by those who have reached the limit of passion."
Then, Vajratārā shall correctly explain the ritual manual for the sādhanas and fire offerings, which are the armor for accomplishing all desired aims.

Now, these are the preliminary verses: *Oṃ namo ratnatrayāya*. *Oṃ nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tathāgatāya*. *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture sarvaduṣṭān mama kṛte je stambhaya stambhaya mohaya bandhaya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ sarvaduṣṭastambhani tāre svāhā*.
In the central location of the *ma mdo* maṇḍala, one should meditate on the goddess Tārā, who has eight arms and four faces, and is fully adorned with all ornaments.
Regarding her four faces: the eastern is yellow, the southern is blue, the western is red, and the northern is white.

*Caṇḍabīja* is *rājikā* (black mustard). "It is not a limb of enlightenment" means that it is certainly not a constituent part of enlightenment. [She] meditates on the appearance of golden color, blazing with the characteristics of a young woman; she is adorned with the crowns of the four Buddhas born from the empowerment of the Vajra Sun.
With a body approaching youth, shimmering like golden earrings,
she sits upon a seat of various lotuses, adorned with red rays of light. Her right hands hold a vajra, a noose, and likewise a conch, while her left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel.
The female [deity] holds an utpala lotus with a vajra hook in her left hand;
by means of the vajra cross-legged posture, the third stage is to be accomplished.
To the east is Puṣpā, white in color and enchanting.
Born from the syllable Oṃ, her hands are covered with garlands of flowers; she has two arms and a single face, and is fully adorned with various ornaments.
To her right is Dhūpa Tārā, possessing a beautiful dark-colored form.
The hand joined with the hand of Spoṅ;
adorned with all ornaments, to the west is the goddess Mārīcī, holding a lamp-stand in her hand;
the great one, beautifully adorned in yellow, with swaying yellow earrings.

In the north is Gandhāri Tārā; her hands reach out to the very source of fragrance. This goddess, with a complexion like the color of blood, should be visualized at the heart of the maṇḍala. With her iron hook and other implements fully extended, one should contemplate her guarding the gates there. Above is Uṣṇīṣavijayā, and below one should visualize Aparājitā. Having visualized the wheel and the nāgas, one should emanate and raise the couch. Oṃ tāre trū trū re trū.

"RE SVĀHĀ. With these ten syllables, one should meditate with great diligence upon the ten goddesses who abide in the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) for the sake of perfectly accomplishing all fruits. This mantra is supreme and transcendent; it is honored by all the Buddhas. It is a fierce transformation through recitation, as explained in the *Vajrapañjara*. One should empower the hem of a garment seven times with this mantra, using a knot.

Furthermore, even when walking through terrifying forests, one will not be carried away; by the mere recollection [of this mantra], one is protected from tigers, thieves, deep waters, narrow paths, lions, snakes, scorpions, bears, wild boars, hyenas, and so forth. With this mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations into a fire of utpala flowers, reciting: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre amukaṃ me*.

WA SHĀMMA NAYA SVĀHĀ. If one recites this mantra twice over the feathers of a peacock’s tail three times and hides it in the enemy’s house, they will be driven away within seven days. OṂ TĀRE TUTTĀRE CALA PRACALA ŚIGHRAM GĀMIDEVA DATTAṂ AVAŚYATĀYA HŪṂ PHAṬ. Furthermore, there is another application: OṂ TĀRE TURE ĀMUKHA BHINHA.

NA KU M'A R'I MA TYA MUNGB'A HE NA TA SYA PE TA PHRA TSHTAMTU ME SVĀHĀ. One should perform the burnt offering (*homa*) by burning *spratshil*, wrathful seeds (*bīja*), intoxicants, leaves of *āśvakā*, and flowers, together with ghee, honey, and molasses, in a quantity of one thousand. This is highly auspicious for the attainment of the siddhi of a maiden; at that time, within seven days, the yogin shall obtain his own desire.

One obtains the daughter of a paṇḍita. Furthermore, one who applies the following ritual—*pāntāre tu ttāre tu re āmu kha bhiṅgha nāmasasthā anta āḥ karṣaya manti ke jaḥ*—and performs this recitation while offering five thousand *rīti* flowers together with naturally occurring blossoms and incense, will summon even the daughters of the protectors of beings (*jagatpāla*). Then...

One should draw the supreme Guru, the two-armed, one-faced Bhagavatī who is about to engage in union with another, holding a hook and an *utpala* flower together with a noose; having made offerings before her, one should recite the mantra while performing the visualization from the verse beginning with "These flowers are auspicious for the field," and so forth, until the lake has been drawn out: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture samu...*

"KĪ MA ME PA SI TĀM, SVAPNĀṂ KṚTHĀ HŪṂ PHAṬ. It will come five thousand times. Having bound it with a noose and drawn it in with a hook, one should perform the rite of accomplishment; one should imagine [the deity] beneath the feet and strike in the manner of a slave-girl. Furthermore, regarding the method for causing [someone] to sneeze: having empowered the mantra of Tārā seven times, [one applies it] to one's own two eyes with eye-medicine.

One should study and enter into the presence of those of the royal caste. Then, the king will treat one with respect as if he were his own disciple, will not act contrary [to one's wishes], and will grant favors.

One should speak pleasant words and ensure that even the lowliest servants behave correctly and that those who are angry are brought under control; this is the direct perception accompanied by wonder. Then, furthermore, as for the application: having recited the mantra of Tārā one hundred and eight times, one should grind the teeth of a donkey and [the seeds of] the *arka* tree with the oil of red-colored goats. From the *bala* tree...

One should collect the medicinal eye-remedies *añjana* from the "Flame-Burning Tree" (*sdong bu rab tu sbar ma*). One should apply the "Eye-Disease" (*mig sman*), "Vajra-Sun," and "Vajra-Dharma-Delight" using the finest horse. These should be mixed with ashes and applied as an ointment to the eyes; by the gaze of the Vajra-Eye, whatever is looked upon will become blissful. If the hand of Padmanarteśvara does not descend, then at that time, I shall seize Tārā, and I shall slay the Blessed Buddhas.

It is so. Furthermore, there is another application: having taken the flesh of a childless woman and empowered it seven times with the *dhāraṇī* of Tārā, one mixes it with the root of a *rājika* plant and cow urine; by applying a drop [of this mixture] to the forehead, whomever one looks upon will be brought under one's control. Furthermore, there is another application: [using] the insect from the belly... the *dhāraṇī*.

One should perform the sevenfold recitation; having performed it together with the vajra, one should place the tooth-stick on the forehead and give it to the practitioner. When he has consumed this supreme application, he shall not abandon [the practice], nor shall he find pleasure elsewhere, nor go to another [place].

One should also abandon one’s own master. Then, another application follows: having smeared oneself with a large amount of human fat, one should recite the mantra of Tārā and meditate upon her. At the conclusion of the recitation, having applied garlic to the impurities and made them into a paste, one gives it to whomever [is desired]; that person will not even vomit it up. Then, another application follows: at the time of the moon's conjunction... Tārā...

One should recite the mantra of Tārā and perform the ritual service; then, taking the worldly lord produced therefrom, one should grind it with conch-shell powder and give it to Pradīptā. As long as she previously followed [the practitioner], she will thereafter become engaged in further application. By means of that desired fruit, one should recite the mantra of Tārā eight times over the horse-necked [conch].

If one is bound by a curse from a relative, recite this mantra: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture āmuka-śyabandha-nāmamukām kuru maḥ svāhā*. Write this mantra on an *arka* leaf, inserting the name of the person to be liberated within it, and place it inside a small clay vessel; they will be released from their bonds. Then, the source of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)...

It shall be explained: by merely meditating upon this, one will overcome all adversaries. One should visualize the goddess with two arms and one face, white in complexion and captivating the mind, with hair half-bound, perfectly seated upon a very white lotus. In her two hands, she holds a white-colored lotus; and in her left [hand], the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Abiding in the vajra posture, one should meditate on her, adorned with all ornaments, within the mandala of the navel. Having generated the Samayasattva born from *Oṃ*, one should meditate on the Jñānasattva; by practicing yoga for six months, one will attain the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). By applying oneself for seven nights, [the result is attained].

It causes one to understand all treatises. Through the application of reciting one hundred thousand [times], one will produce one hundred verses every single day. Without great exertion, one will also retain one hundred texts. In that regard, the mantra-verse is: *Oṃ pi tsu bi tsu pra jñā vārddhani*.

*Dzra la dzvā la me dhā va rdha ni, dhi ri dhi ri buddhi va rdha ni svā hā.* Having empowered sour fruit that has not been previously extracted by reciting this mantra seven times, one should sprinkle it seven times over [the fruit]. Whoever drinks this for six months will come to possess great wisdom (*prajñā*). Then, the characteristics of the Vajra Master...

The one who has correctly explained the *Tattva*, And by whom the mantras have been properly attended to, Will certainly achieve success as a practitioner. Possessing leisure and endowed with the profound Dharma, Accompanied by expertise in all fields of knowledge, Knowing the fire offerings (*homa*), the maṇḍala, and the mantras, Having mastered consecration (*pratisthā*) and the ritual cakes (*bali*), Fully cognizant of the ten *tattvas*, A protector who observes the conduct of the Śrāvakas, Devoted to the stages of mantra practice, And possessing a beautiful form.

Seeing which brings joy, it is endowed with the drawing of mandalas and recitation; it is the vanquisher of root downfalls. Through the application of mantra and the protection of the body, it brings happiness to the worlds. Together with the Guru, whoever reviles the Guru—any person who reviles the Guru—will be tormented in the great hells. Just as Vajra Lokarāja is a Buddha...

All should first make offerings; through the vajra pavilion, one should thus perform service for the guru. Whoever, out of great delusion, steps upon the guru’s shadow, or his woman, his shoes, his seat, or his bed, that person holds a razor in their hand. Any disciple who has been properly empowered and yet transgresses the guru’s command will come to ruin in this world and in the next.

By means of the application of movement and illusion, one who speaks falsely through deception will be unable [to attain success] and will suffer from great diseases such as pulmonary consumption, and will be reborn in the hells and other realms. A disciple who understands this should perfect the service and honor of the guru; by strictly guarding the guru’s command, the extensive accomplishments (*siddhi*) will be attained. One should always partake of the feast offering (*gaṇacakra*); [one should perform] pacification and so forth.

Exhort them! First, perform the Dharma teaching for the Saṅgha; honor the Guru as a Buddha. Present offerings to the Guru, and thereafter to the entire assembly. Having reflected upon my own activities, I shall accomplish them through this ritual. Adorned with all the ornaments of the limbs, and taking up the vajra and bell, I shall offer the *bali* at the crossroads of the path. [Offer] flowers, incense, lamps, and—

To the right, [place] conch shells and so forth for scent; to the left, the vessel for the mantra-offering water (*mantrapūjā-argha*). One should place the vessels in front. According to the aforementioned ritual for the foot-washing water, one should perform the offering with flowers, incense, and so forth, in their proper sequence, using offerings such as lamps and the like. By the manner of transforming the flowers and the manner of scattering the incense, by the offering of the lamp with its wick and by the application of the unguents—[if one offers thus], it will be excellent.

Questioned by the body of the consort, with the left hand placed upon the left [shoulder], the garland-bearer is the ḍākinī of the garland; with song, she sings the *hūṃ* pledge-song; by drawing up the knees, that is the dance itself. These supreme [practices] are unsurpassed; they please all the Buddhas. By making offerings to the Buddhas, one makes offerings [to them]; the siddhi of desire will be accomplished through recitation and meditation. Manifest...

Delighted, always crossing to the far shore of saṃsāra, according to the command of the Vajradākinī: these are the unsurpassed offerings. Offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth, performed by those who abide in worldly conduct, are not the supreme offering; they are not the branches of enlightenment themselves. White is said to bring about pacification (*śānti*); yellow is the method for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*); red is for empowerment (*vaśya*) and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*).

For black magic, [the flower] is black; for pacification, it is white; for enrichment, yellow; for the vajra [subjugation], black; for power and summoning, red is excellent. For any yogin who has not received empowerment, who has not entered the maṇḍala, who has not witnessed the consecration, and who has not performed the fire offering—his supreme siddhi will exist neither in this world nor in the next.

MED, [requested by the preceptor: "In this [state], there is no birth into a [specific] caste; one should meditate upon all the Buddhas. For whoever has not attained enlightenment, they will be born again and again in the station of a universal monarch (cakravartin), or even as the Lord of the World (Īśvara) himself."

They proceed directly to the abodes of the pure, and those with intelligence are born in Sukhāvatī, among the ḍākinīs, or in Tuṣita. As for whatever is accomplished here in this world—what need is there to speak of that Buddha?

This great lord of the three realms is not pervaded by death or old age; Brahmā, Śakra, as well as the fierce ones, Rāhu, Agni, Vāyu, the gods of desire, and even those possessing the power of flight—all these become his retinue. Likewise, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, kinnaras, and those who roam the sky—they too will undoubtedly become his retinue. This is...

The Self-Arisen Blessed One, having beheld the world to be disciplined, manifests these many forms for the sake of sentient beings: turning the wheel of Dharma, manifesting the lineage and the practice for enlightenment, likewise ascending to the heavens, departing from the household life, adopting the state of renunciation, taking birth, and demonstrating parinirvāṇa. Buddha, [you act] for the sake of sentient beings.

Desiring to grant protection, the Buddha performs his dance in various forms; even within the lineages of rabbits, tigers, lions, and elephants, he is born through the mudrā of compassion and a mind intent on benefiting others. Through the display of illusory women, he teaches the Dharma to those possessed by desire. The illusory woman is the Buddha himself; she clears away all illusions. [She is] Prajñāpāramitā...

In the form of a woman, she always dwells in perfect purity; abiding as a great illusion, she bestows the supreme awakening of a Buddha. Unwavering, pure, and free from deceit, she always transcends desire and grants even the highest siddhis. Regarding form, qualities, or wealth, there is no woman who possesses such longing as Vajrarāgacittā for her own bliss.

Myang bar ldan, the person endowed with ethical discipline, who does not transgress the commands of the Sugata, who honors the guru and possesses compassion—this is the thorough revelation of Hevajra. Then, with this king of praises, the yoginī Nairātmyā, the principal, and the ḍākinīs made this supplication: "Homage and praise to Vajra Hatred! Homage and praise to Vajra Delusion!"

O Vajra of Hatred, please take pity on me; O Vajra of Desire, please grant me your favor. You who possess the great mind and great envy, the foremost of all vajra samaya-holders, the accomplisher of all activities—O you who possess the vajra, may you all be pleased! Then the Blessed One, abiding in the samaya of all dakinis, uttered this melody: "A new, beautiful, and perfectly measured thread..."

With pure mind, one who possesses wisdom should lay out the lines for the mandala called *He*. In this regard, this is the commitment (*samaya*) of the request made by the great disciple: "O Guide of the Mandala, please explain the mandala that has arisen from Vajrasattva—the abode of all Tathāgatas and the peace of all Tathāgatas. These are the requests made to the Vajra of the Mandala.

Through the samādhi called "Supreme Victory," I am the glorious one whose power is compassion. I am the practitioner of the protective wheel; with the vajra, my body is made radiant. From my body, speech, and mind, emanations are projected. If anyone should transgress this, they will undoubtedly perish right here. Those who are sluggish in body or in some way deficient shall arise from the wisdom of great bliss and be born with the very nature of Vajrasattva—be heedful!

The great gates are renowned as being one-eighth of the wheel itself. The divine canopy of the empty chamber should be made the same size as the gate. The pediment and the side-walls should be half the size of the gate. The *vedī* (pedestal) should likewise be made so; the *dava* (canopy) pedestal should be one *veda* (fourth) [of that]. First is the line of Brahmā, and second is the boundary line.

Dang yang, for the third [line], the four [sides] of the four [corners]; one should draw the lines clearly. Having set aside two parts of the Brahma-line, one should draw [the lines] in six parts. Then, having set aside the measurement of the door, one should draw [the lines] in nine parts. Regarding that, it is as follows:

This is the samaya for purification: Oṃ Khaṃ Hūṃ Bhūṃ. Regarding this, the following is the invocation of the wisdom [deities]: Oṃ me di ni badzrī bhā va badzra bandha hūṃ. Regarding this, the following is the samaya for marking with lines: Oṃ samaya sūtra mati krama hūṃ. Regarding this, the following is the samaya for drawing the colored powders: This is the purity of the *dharmadhātu*; it liberates the realm of sentient beings. Kyé yi...

The Great Vajra King shall cause the maṇḍala to be drawn. At the northeast (īśāna) corner, one should draw Śarabha; at the southeast (agni) corner, a bhikṣu; at the southwest (nairṛtya) corner, the wheel of Dharma; and at the northwest (vāyu), a vajra should be drawn. A hook should be drawn in the east; at the southern gate, a noose itself; at the western gate, likewise a bell; and in the north, a vajra-gong. In the center, a white skull-cup.

POṆI: Drawing the various types of mudrās, then, by means of the application of the vajra hearth through the King who holds the mudrā, from the preparation of the vajra oblation materials, it is taught that a circular shape brings about pacification (śānti). For enrichment (puṣṭi), the form is like a pond; for magnetizing (vaśya), it is like a half-moon; for summoning (ākarṣaṇa), it has the shape of a hook; and for killing (māraṇa) and hatred (dveṣa)...

The *la la ni* is like the expanse of space. Likewise, when one who is unfortunate performs the rite of expulsion, by means of the application of impaired limbs—using *candana*, *agaru* wood, and other fragrant roots—one kindles the fire of the limbs for the *homa* offering and subsequently performs the summoning once again. *ao ae hye hi mahābhūta deva riṣi dvidja sattva grihītvā āhuti māheśvari*

In this very place, one should summon with the hook (*aṅkuśa*), cause [the deity] to enter by means of the noose (*pāśa*), bind the limbs with the chain (*śṛṅkhalā*), and bring [them] under control by ringing the bell (*ghaṇṭā*). Having performed the eightfold offerings, such as the mirror and so forth, and having completed the ritual of the drinking water (*argha*), one should again gratify the fire through the application of ghee and other substances. In this regard, this is the samaya of the vajra *argha* offering.

Furthermore, this is the samaya-mantra for the cooling of the feet: *oṃ sarvapāpān dahana vajrāya svatvasya sarvapāpān daha svāhā*. Furthermore, this is the mantra of the samaya for the dissolution of all substances to be burned: *oṃ vajranala mahābhūta jvalaya sarvabhāsmin kuru sarvaduḥkhāni hūṃ*.

PHAT, DRI SHYA DZAḤ: HŪM BAM HOḤ: SAMAYA STVAM Ā HĀM. Having thus invited the deity one desires, [recite]: OṂ ĀE HYE HI BHAGAVĀN ĀBHAKṢAṆĀ SAMAYE NI TSĀ ARGHANTU SAM PRATĪCCHA PUJA JÑĀNA DĀ PRASIDDHA ME. Regarding that, this is the pledge of joy: OṂ KRITO BAḤ SARVA SATVĀRTHAḤ SIDDHI RDDATTĀYA THĀNU GACCHA DHĀM BUDDHA VIŚĀYĀM BUNA RĀGAMAṆĀYA MUḤ.
The eighth chapter: on the postures, the applications of various activities, and the fire offering (homa). ||o||

Then the King Vajradhara said: "The consecration of Vajrasattva, abiding by way of worldly convention, shall be taught in brief. *Dhvaninirgūḍha* means being free from the clamor and noise of people."
First, one should hold the consort, desire to ring the bell,
and through the yoga of extending the right leg, brandish a vajra with the right hand;
then, letting out a piercing cry, one should bind the throat with a garment.

One should place a vessel filled with precious medicinal substances; "precious" refers to the five jewels, and "medicinal substances" refers to the five medicines. This is also indicative of the five grains.

Oṃ de wa pi tsu badzra dhi tiṣṭha | Oṃ mo ha ra ti ā dhi tiṣṭha | Oṃ dve śa ra ti ā dhi tiṣṭha | Oṃ rā ga ra ti ā dhi tiṣṭha | Oṃ badzra ra ti ā dhi tiṣṭha | Oṃ badzra gū rī ā karṣaya jaḥ | Oṃ badzra tsūrī pra peśaya hūṃ | Oṃ badzra petālī bandhaya bāṃ | Oṃ badzra ghasmarī vaśyaṃ kuru hoḥ | This is the ritual for summoning primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

*Oṃ deva*, etc. The intended meaning is as follows: by means of the mass of rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one should attract the deities such as Hevajra together with Gaurī and the others who are pleased by the mantra, cause them to enter the vases, bind them, and subjugate them, while reciting the mantra beginning with *oṃ*. The mantras *oṃ moharatī* and so forth are to be understood as belonging to Locanā and the other [consorts] for the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the vases. However, the mantras *oṃ vajragaurī* and so forth belong to Gaurī and the others for the purpose of attracting the deities and so on.
The five voids and the five hairs, and especially the five perfumes, [should be used].

One should eject the body into the fire; the water offerings and so forth should be performed as before, or else that very [offering] should be applied. Having first ejected [the body], one should consecrate it.
One should brandish the three vajras at the three places—the eyes and so forth—to dispel ignorance and the other afflictions.

"Again, by that very [method]," and so forth. The meaning is that at the time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), everything should be performed as previously described. Now, in order to show the empowerment of the eyes and so forth for the deities who have been consecrated, he says: "In the eyes and so forth," and so on. "By means of one's own family (*kula*), one should begin with the offerings and so forth in sequence; from one's own heart, one should visualize the gnosis (*jñāna*), and perform the secret offering (*guhyabalidāna*) for the Buddhas to abide [therein]."

"One should undertake the offerings and so forth in sequence"—this is the summary. "The state of gnosis" refers to the Gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*). "The Buddhas" refers to those who are established [in their seats].
"By means of the yoga of the Gnosis-Vajra, one should emanate the goddesses of worship in sequence;
having visualized the supreme bodhicitta, one should properly commence the praise of the Buddhas."
"Supreme bodhicitta" refers to the form of the ḍākinīs and so forth. "By the nature of all things, emptiness and compassion are inseparable."
You are completely surrounded by a host of yoginīs;
you are one who has attained the supreme satisfaction of your own heart;
you have brought to fulfillment all beings of the moving and non-moving worlds.
With a heart of compassion, you bring sentient beings to buddhahood;
through illusory emanations, you expand the vajra.
Glorious Heruka, rejoice with your vajra mind!

"Of all phenomena," and so forth, up to "Heruka, O Vajra"—this is the praise. "By means of the union with the vajra seal, one should meditate on the meditation of the vajra; having taken up the syllable of the vajra, one should meditate on the vajra mandala."

"Vajrācchaṭā," and so forth. Having formed the vajra-bind with the two arms, and having made a hook with the index fingers while reciting the mantra *vajrasamāja jaḥ 2*, one should snap the fingers with the middle and thumb fingers. "The meditation on the vajra-abode" (*vajrabhavanabhāvanā*) means the meditation on both the vajra and the abode; the meaning is that by means of the snap accompanied by the syllable *hūṃ*, one should instantly perceive the maṇḍala of the support and the supported. The "vajra-syllable" is the syllable *yaṃ*. [Remaining text: "Abiding in the center of the vajra-maṇḍala, one should clearly visualize the vajra-aggregate."

Then, one should visualize the vajra offering. Through the application of the vajra tongue, one should perform the purification and scattering (*vāsagorṇa*) with the vajra mantra, having caused the Buddhas to enter the vajra [mandala].

[The sequence is: the vajra-mandala, the wind-mandala, the vajra-heap, and the fire-mandala; thus, "vajra-cooking" refers to the purification of substances in the proper manner through the stages of blazing, heating, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having caused the vajra-Buddhas to enter," the words "into the *dharmodaya* and so forth" are to be supplied as an ellipsis.
The Blessed One, the Vajra who tastes the flavor of vajra-nectar, spoke these words:
"Having reached the center of the expanse of space,
one who desires the siddhi of the Buddha should, by means of the power of the five-pronged [vajra] drawn there, pierce the Buddhas with the kīla."

"By means of the five-pronged binding" means that one should fashion one's own vajra into the form of a five-pronged vajra and thereby effect a binding at the door of the lotus of the consort (*prajñā*). "Residing in the center of the space-element" means that having seen the Buddhas turned away in the sky, they are cast into the interior of the consort’s lotus by means of the mouth. "In the beautiful city of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), if through the application of the vajra-fist no siddhi is granted, then Vajrasattva should be slain."
"By means of the application of the vajra-fingers" refers to the application of the eight stakes in the form of Vajrayamāri.
*Oṃ du ru du ru, tschinda tschinda, hūṃ hūṃ.* Thus the Blessed One spoke these words regarding the great striking with the stake: "Vajra!"
Abiding in the center of the ma-mo maṇḍala, one should visualize Hayagrīva.
Upon his head-ornament is Vajradharma; as described in the Mahāmudrā, he holds a red lotus upon his crown. His body is red in color and possesses great power.
The Ritual of the Non-dual Union of the White [Deity] (Gos dkar gnyis med sbyor ba’i las), adorned with sixteen arms.
"Red" (*raktām*) means being passionately devoted for the sake of sentient beings. "The body of the deity" refers to that which is designated by the term *mahāmudrā*.
"Having observed" (*vīkṣya*) means one should behold it. "With a mind intent on the propitiation of vigor" (*vīryārādhanacetasā*) means with an intention for propitiation preceded by vigor.
The right face is black, while the left is as beautiful as the stainless moon; the first [face] should be known as red, and the remaining faces resemble bees.
Having eight faces and four legs, Vajradharma is of great majesty.
Through the continuous flow of great passion, the four māras are brought into equipoise.
Abiding in the center of the ma-mo maṇḍala, one should bring to mind Vajravairocana;
visualize him holding a vajra as a crown ornament, his body white in color and of great brilliance.
With sixteen hands, eight faces, and four feet, he is terrifying.
Holding the wheel of Dharma upon his crown, following after great passion,
and through the union with the two eyes, this very one causes fear to be feared.
The first face is white, adorned with black and red;
the remaining faces resemble bees.
Abiding in the center of the *māmakī* maṇḍala, one should clearly visualize Vajrasūrya.
Visualize the one who holds the precious jewel of the mind; he is Vajra Splendor, of great radiance, with sixteen arms, eight faces, and four feet—the Terrifying One.
He holds the precious jewel of the mind upon his crown, blazing with a brilliance like molten gold.
The first face is yellow, while the right one appears blue;
the left is like the moonlight, and the remaining faces resemble bees. Abiding in the center of the maṇḍala of the Mothers, one should visualize the supreme horse.
Visualize him holding a sword as a head ornament; his eyes are like blue utpala lotuses.
He has eight faces and four legs, and is adorned with sixteen arms.
His first face is dark blue, having the terrifying form of a horse.
The right face is black in color, while the left is as stainless and beautiful as the moon.
Holding the sword of accomplishments upon his crown, the remaining faces resemble bees.
This mudrā of the vajra-sun and horse itself is the form of Tārā.
The two hands of the goddesses are described: they hold a curved knife and a skull-cup.
O Vajra, supreme mandala!
The sword is indeed eternal, and the mirror is likewise for the benefit [of beings].
The horse’s neck is draped with fine cloth,
its body is like a golden vajra-sun,
and this supreme steed is swift in its gait.
One who desires the fruit of Buddhahood should constantly and perpetually offer the gift of supreme benefit to the guru.
I am the Fortunate Vajrasattva;
the Fortunate Muni Vairocana;
the Fortunate Glorious Lokeshvara.

Then, the Sovereign King Skal bzang nyi ma bdun rgyal po, the Supreme Vajradhara of the Three Bodies, the Lord of Secrets, spoke this supreme samaya of the Vajradhara: *Oṃ dhara dhara, dhāraya dhāraya, marda marda, vajradhrīka phaṭ svāhā*.

Then, while the Great Mantra was being explained, Vajrajanma-karuṇa became terrified and struck with fear, and he offered up the supreme vajra-siddhi. Thereupon, the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the form of Vajradharma and uttered this Hayagrīva mantra: *Oṃ vajradharma samaya stvām hulu hulu oṃ ārolika phaṭ svāhā*.
