Then...

When this was explained, the great Vajradharma became terrified and struck with fear, and he offered the siddhi of the Dharma. Then, the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption known as Vairocanavajra and spoke this mantra of benefit: Oṃ svā śvataṃ paraṃ svā śvate ārye hi jina jike phaṭ svāhā.

Then, by merely explaining this, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas became bewildered and terrified. Thereupon, the Buddhas bestowed their accomplishments (*siddhi*). Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption known as the "Precious Sun" (*Ratnasūrya*) and uttered this Vajra Splendor mantra: *Oṃ vajrasūrya-tamo-vighnana samaya stvām āḥ hāṃ ratna*.

*Dhṛika phaṭ svāhā!* Then, by merely explaining this, the Great Radiant Vajra Splendor became terrified and bewildered, and he offered the siddhi of the Sun. Thereupon, the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called Amoghasiddhi-vajra and spoke this supreme horse-vajra mantra: *Phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ!*

HI HI HI PRAJÑĀDHṚK PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. Then, by the mere mention of this, the Vajrāmoghasambhava became terrified and fainting; he then granted the siddhi of Amogha. That very mandala of the Buddha is like the crescent moon of the Vajra-holder, resembling the lotus of Vajradharma, and bestows the sun-like wish-fulfilling jewel. Of that which is called the Supreme Steed (Ucchuṣma):

In all [directions] there are three ships. With the great mudrā of Vajrasattva, the very mudrā of benefit, and the great mudrā of the Vajra-Dharma, she who radiates light from the Jewel-Pinnacle, and the great mudrā of Amoghasiddhi—adorned with bone ornaments, wearing a tiger-skin skirt, and with hair bound in a skull-crest—by the heroic beings striving in worship, [these are offered].
Having seen one with red eyes who is full of passion, one should meditate through the union of passion, by means of the application of Mahāmudrā.
This is the ninth chapter, on the accomplishment of various activities.
|| Navamaḥ paricchedaḥ || |||
Then the Vajradhara King shall explain the characteristics of conduct:
by means of the application of the Vajra Conduct,
one should correctly assume the vajra-mudrā— namely, the wheel, the earring, and so forth.
Adorned with peacock feathers and the like,
they shall go to the very edge of the great forest as great beings;
wandering through the groves as beggars, they shall receive fine food and ornaments, which those [beings] will give out of fear and terror.
All the families of the Lord of the Forest (Vajrapāṇi) shall become his retinue.
Whatever beings are born, or will be born in all births,
they shall see with vajra-eyes through the yoga of the Vajra of Delusion (moha).

"By the eye-vajra" means by the eye that is unattached and unimpeded in form. "Just as whatever sound is clearly proclaimed remains within the range of the ear, so too [does it arise] from the application of the hatred-vajra. Regarding "the path of the three realms is delightful": it is the path of the three realms that is experienced with joy. Regarding "whatever sound is clearly proclaimed": it refers to the sound that is thoroughly resounded. Regarding "remaining within the range of the ear": it is as if it were situated right before the ear. From the application of the hatred-vajra, [this occurs].
The ṛṣi, through his supernormal knowledge,
heard: "The great mind of all sentient beings, possessing characteristics like a mirror,
will be known by the vajra-mind as clearly as a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand."
"The great mind of all sentient beings": the nominative case is used here in the sense of the genitive.
Throughout thousands of millions of births, one’s own lineage will be remembered through the vajra-yoga; it will be recollected as clearly as the three suns.
By means of various illusory nets, this shall bring about illumination.

Through the application of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), one will attain the superknowledges of a Buddha. "Peace through the very [state of] passion; expansion by the Vajra-Sun;
empowerment by the Vajra-Dharma; and slaying by the Vajrasattva.
Through a peaceful mind, there is peace; and one should correctly undertake empowerment."

"One should commence the consecration" means: one who is engaged in the yoga of a white deity such as Vairocana and so forth, having struck down the one to be accomplished—who is situated within a water-maṇḍala at one's own heart, or who resides within a water-maṇḍala upon the lotus of the consort—by means of deities accompanied by white nectar-flasks, and having consecrated him, one should perceive him as consisting of the atoms of the white deity.
"With an expansive mind, perform the expansion; one should intensely meditate on clouds raining jewels.
With a mind of attachment, one should summon a maiden and partake [of her]."

"With a nourishing mind" means with an exceedingly expansive consciousness. One who possesses the yoga of Vajrasūrya should, as before, visualize the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) situated within the Maheśvara maṇḍala, consecrate them with the nectar from yellow vases, and visualize them as consisting of atoms composed of yellow deities; then one should behold a rain of various jewels falling upon their house. Having attracted a maiden, one should enjoy her with a mind of passion. The practitioner of the Vajradharma yoga, having duly attracted [the object], should consecrate her with red vases, bring the person to be accomplished under control, and thus fulfill their desire.
"Rain shall fall from my mouth, and with a malicious mind one should perform the act of killing;
for the rite of seizing, it is white, while from the second birth [the rite] is Brahman itself.
"With a malicious mind" means with a cruel disposition; by means of the yoga of the blue deity, having caused a rain of fire to fall upon the victim, one should effect the killing.
Even from the son of the God of Wealth (Kubera), one who is not purified becomes a *rāmbha*;
from the joyous consort of the Lord of Makaras (*makaradhvaja*), through the application of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*),
all of those are consumed.
With a mind of intense joy, one is not defiled by desire;
at the end, *svāhā* is for pacification, while during the time of enrichment, it is *poṣaṭ*.
At the end, *hūṃ phaṭ* is for killing; for magnetizing and summoning, there are *jāḥ* and *hrīḥ*.
"Then the Vajradhara King [spoke]; for the sake of perfectly accomplishing the Vajra-Ḍākinī and the Vajrapañjara, the Muni uttered these words.
Regarding the question "What did he say?", the compiler says "iti vāṅmunir iti" and so forth, and demonstrates that very point with the verse beginning "girī... and so on.
In mountain ranges and medicinal groves adorned with flowers and fruits, sitting in the vajra posture, I shall worship the Guru-Buddha.
I take refuge in the Three Jewels; I confess all my misdeeds individually.
Rejoicing in the virtue of all beings, I shall hold fast to the mind of enlightenment.
In the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly, I take refuge until I reach enlightenment.
In order to perfectly accomplish the welfare of myself and others, I shall generate the bodhicitta.
Having generated the supreme mind of awakening, I shall take all sentient beings as my guests;
I shall practice the delightful and sublime conduct of awakening, and may I attain buddhahood for the benefit of the world.
By means of the four abodes of Brahmā, I shall rest from mental fatigue.

"Abiding externally in the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) is the samaya of the Vajra Protection. This means that one should perform the meditation on ultimate bodhicitta, which is the meditation on emptiness.
"By means of the yoga of wrath" means by means of the pride of wrath.
"By means of the practice of truth and falsehood, one is not defiled by investigation;
through the yoga of the unarisen, one is proclaimed here as being born. Regarding "by the yoga of the immortal" (*amṛtayogena*):

they are called "immortal" (*amṛta*) because they do not die; these are Vajra-hūṃkāra and the others. Their "yoga" is the act of making them the central leader [in the maṇḍala]; that is the meaning. Alternatively, the "yoga of the immortal" is the radiation of Amṛtakundalin; the connection is that one should dispel obstacles by means of that.
Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham.
In the center of the expanse of space, one should visualize a variegated vajra;
through the union of ten Hūṃs, the ten wrathful deities are sequentially emanated.

"Situated in the midst of the space-element" means situated in the center of the arising of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, Vighnāntaka, the wrathful Takkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, Acala, and Mahābala—

The *Gtsug tor gdugs* (Uṣṇīṣacakravartin) is white; those dwelling beneath the vajra feet and those dwelling beneath the nectar feet should all be meditated upon through the visualization of wrathful deities by means of the application of nectar.
Having visualized [the deity] pervading the hundred directions, one should expel the obstructing spirits.
One should meditate on the vajra mandala abiding in the center of the expanse of space; one should meditate on the mandala of light.

The vajra-maṇḍala is the wind-maṇḍala; the ray-maṇḍala is the fire-maṇḍala. Abiding in the center of the maṇḍala of *me yi* (the letter *me*), one should again meditate on water. Abiding in the center of the water-maṇḍala, the practitioner should meditate on the great element of fire.
Upon the great empowerment mandala, one should likewise meditate upon oneself.
Having visualized the abode from the seed-syllable, one should examine that vajra mandala;
it should be thoroughly examined in five aspects.

"One should meditate on the reflected image of the Hero (sattvabimba) arisen from the five wisdoms; one should meditate on the person of the Vidyā arisen from Vajrasattva. Regarding "arisen from the five wisdoms" (*pañcajñānasamudbhūta*): it means produced with the intrinsic nature of the five wisdoms. "The reflected image of the Hero" (*sattvabimba*) refers to the body of Vajrasattva. To the question "From what has it arisen?", he says: "arisen from Vajrasattva" (*vajrasattvasamudbhūta*). "Vajra" is the emblem (*cihna*); "sattva" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). The meaning is that it is produced from those two.

Regarding "the *ḍāka*-maṇḍala": like a *ḍāka* is a *ḍāka*, namely Nairātmyā; [it refers to] her maṇḍala. *Oṃ dharmadhātu-vajra-svabhāv-ātmako ’ham*. This is the samādhi called "Vajradhara. Ignorance and the other [afflictions] reside in the eyes and so forth; the three vajras are emanated in the three places.
The Vajra Mind Khachöma, the Vajra Speech Khandro, and the one who dwells at the soles of the feet of the Body—these arise from HŪṂ, ĀḤ, and OṂ.
They constitute the heart-essence of the Bhagavān; they are the White Vajra Water-Lordess.
One should meditate on Nairātmyā, the Vajra Ḍākinī, who occupies the station of Dveṣavajrī at the center of the maṇḍala;
and white Caṇḍikā, the Vetālī, as the gate-keeper Ghasmarī.
Pukkasī is at the mountain peak, Śavarī is at the cemetery, and Caṇḍālī is assigned to the border.
Above, she is explained as Khecarī; below, likewise, she is Bhūcarī.
In the center is Nairātmyā Ḍākinī; one should meditate on them as the very maṇḍala of the Ḍākinīs.
Just as Bodhivajra made great offerings to the Buddha, so too,
for the sake of my complete protection, grant me the Vajra of Space; bestow the great vajra empowerment, which is prostrated to by the three realms.
"May that which arises from the locus of the three secrets of all Buddhas be bestowed.
This is the meditative absorption called "The Vajra of Supplication for the Empowerment of Wisdom.
To the powerful person of the consort, [he offers] the crown of his own tutelary deity.
One should perform the mandala empowerment, as well as the praises, offerings, and so forth;

likewise, one should perform the insertion of the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*). Then, having tasted the vajra-nectar with the tongue, one should recite the mantras of the practitioner through the application of inner recitation.
This is the twelfth chapter, titled "The Emergence of Yoginīs. || 12 || |||o||

"In one's own self" means from one's own body. Then, the bodhisattvas, Maitreya and the others, each gave rise to this thought: "Bhagavān, how should the Yoginī-tantra be practiced? Vajradhara replied:
The method of the perfection of wisdom is explicitly designated as "Yoginī.
Because it teaches reality through the supreme application of Mahāmudrā,
the *Vajrapañjara* of the Yoginīs is explained as the *Yoginī Tantra*.
The method for all the *pāramitās* will be accomplished through meditative concentration alone. The lake of the ḍākinī Nandavatī,
the sky and the rain of gold, Mahānanda, Ghasmarī,
and the secret syllable that radiates intense joy and play.
The Eight Lineages of the Vajra Dakinis:
"O Vajra Buddhas of the syllable Kyee! The Secret Treasury, the Source of Vajra Nectar, The Chakrasamvara, the Gur, and the Source— These are renowned as the Yogini Tantras."
The Yoga Tantras were correctly explained for the sake of training men;
the Yoginī Tantras were explained for the sake of gathering women. For those of inferior capacity, there are the Kriyā Tantras; and for those beyond that, the Unsurpassed Yoga (Anuttarayoga).
"The supreme yogi among supreme beings—there is no yoga higher than that.
Then the bodhisattvas addressed the Blessed One: "If our own domains are to be investigated, how should other beings investigate what has been spoken by the Buddha?
The Blessed One replied:
Wherever the mind is thoroughly cultivated as emptiness inseparable from compassion,
this is the teaching of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
it is for the purpose of refuting the non-Buddhists and subduing all adversaries.
The meditative concentration called "Proclaiming the Doctrine of One’s Own School.
For the sake of attaining my own enlightenment, and for the sake of delivering others,
it is therefore the teaching of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha as well.
In order to reverse attachment to self-grasping, the means for accomplishing the nature of the dharmadhātu consists of the union of method and wisdom;
that is the teaching of the Buddha.
Regarding "belonging to a self" (*ātmīya*): it means "this belongs to each individual self," which is the sense of "one's own."

"Attained" means they produced [it]. Then, having heard these words of the Blessed One, the Blessed Ones and the Sons of the Victorious One became joyful and spoke these words: "O, how wonderful! The teaching of Samantabhadra, which has arisen from space, shall be heard as an ocean of primordial wisdom through application in the center of space. Then, the King Vajradhara, with the expansion of great bliss, [will hear] all the commitments..."
I shall now explain: those who desire the fruit of Buddhahood should, with joy and delight, perform dances and songs, play musical instruments, and offer incense, garlands, and unguents.

When the King of Knowledge is perfectly accomplished, having grasped bliss as it is, one should enjoy whatever is desired. By abiding in whatever dwelling place, the sublime syllable will be accomplished. Through the preparation of food and drink, and adorned with excellent ornaments, by exerting oneself for a single day, that very reality will be accomplished.
One should always taste one’s own samaya and always make offerings to the Tathāgata.
One should always offer [everything] to the guru; the guru is equal to all the Buddhas.
Just as the Protector Vairocana, and the Holder of the Vajra (Vajradhara) who bestows [attainments], and just as the great ocean of space, so too is the Sage Vajradharma.
Just as the King of the Seven Protectors is described, so too is the Vajra Master spoken of.
Therefore, with all effort, one must never disparage the Great Guru, the Vajra Master,
who is supremely radiant with virtue.
This is the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Vajra Pledge.
|| o || Chapter Thirteen.
Then the Blessed One, the Great Vajra, the Laughing Golden Vajra,
was embraced by the ḍākinī Nairātmyā;
having established himself in the form of Vajra, he revealed the *Bhadracaryā* according to his own desire.
The state of being a vidyādhara who turns the wheel will be accomplished without doubt.

Regarding "the conduct of the auspicious" (*bhadracaritam*): it refers to the conduct—that is, the means of accomplishment—of the "auspicious ones," namely those who have attained the siddhis of pills and so forth. Regarding "of the Vajra": this refers to Hevajra.
Having properly taken the five fragrances, they should be mixed with the five substances.
Having wrapped it with the three metals, one will become a holder of the pill-vidyā (*piṇḍavidyādharin*).

Regarding "the five scents" (*pañcagandha*): this refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five substances (*pañcadravya*), and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*). "Wrapped with the three metals" (*trilohaveṣṭita*) means having wrapped it with the three sheets of gold, silver, and copper; the remainder of the sentence implies that one should place it in the mouth. And the phrase "assuming the form of the Vajra" (*rūpam āsthāya vajrasya*) also applies here.

Having placed a pill, which possesses the *gur gum* and is like the color of the rising sun, into one's mouth, one will become a Vidyādhara of the Sun (*sūryavidyādhara*). This is by means of the very ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) as Vajrasūrya.

Having wrapped it with the three metals while endowed with the five meats, through the excellent application of the Vajrasūrya, accomplishment will be achieved in a single day. "Endowed with the five meats" means accompanied by the five lamps.

When Nandagopa, a specific type of living being, is joined with Red Sandalwood (*candana*) and bound with three iron bands, one becomes a *vidyādhara* of the horse (*aśva-vidyādhara*). [This refers to] the supreme horse through the pride of being one.

Having visualized the various forms of Lokanātha, [an image] the size of a chickpea bone, encircled by a chain of gu-gul resin, will become a holder of the vidyā of Lokanātha. *Lokanātham* means Padmanarteśvara.
This is the samādhi called "The Vajra of Accomplishing the Rite.
Having incinerated the heads of the nāga kings, one should empower them with self-arisen blood.
Through the yoga of the Beneficent Vajra, one will become a master of eye-salve vidyādharas.

"Regarding 'Nāgarāja': [this refers to] the serpent king with two faces. Regarding 'Añjana-vidyādhara': [it refers to one who has applied] collyrium to the eyes. "Possessing the seeds of the Guru, Smearing the fat from a tiger's skin, Through the yoga of the vajra body, One will achieve success in the foot-ointment."

The seed is semen. Regarding the passage beginning with "śārdūla" (tiger): having smeared both feet with tiger-skin oil together with realgar and the seed [semen], the yogin Vairocana becomes accomplished through the application of this foot-ointment; such is the meaning.
"In the center of the mandala of the Armless One, on the slope of the Indra Cave, the yogin Vajrapāda shall thoroughly accomplish the daughters of the gods."

"Anaṅgamaṇḍala," and so forth. This is the collective meaning here: having drawn the maṇḍala called the Protection Circle (*rakṣācakra*) with colored powders in the center of the Indraśaila cave, with Vajrānaṅga as the central deity, one should visualize oneself as that central deity situated therein and give the command to Sumbharāja positioned below by means of the mantra beginning with "Oṃ sumbha."

Sumbha, too, having stationed a second emanation of himself in his own place, enters the netherworld (pātāla) and, having summoned the maidens of the netherworld, delivers them to the practitioner; thus, by meditating for seven days during the three junctions of the day, one shall accomplish the desired goal.
When one approaches the land of Oḍra, by means of the application of the *vajrarakṣasa* (the Vajra-Demon), one will become a *vidyādhara* at one's feet.
Regarding "Oḍradeśa" and so forth: here too, the procedure is exactly as before.

"O Great King Vajrasattva, you should be exhorted again and again; you are like a wish-fulfilling jewel in respect to all accomplishments. (*Vajrasattva* etc. By this, he shows that for the sake of accomplishing *siddhi*, one should meditate upon another deity.
"Vajra, of great and fierce body, with two hands and one face,
making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and seizing a nāga, one should visualize him as black in color.
To show the actual form of Sumbharāja, he says "Sumbhavajra," and so forth.
Having taken up the Vajra-hūṃ-kāra, one should meditate upon it in all its aspects; it is firmly held by Akṣobhya, and the mantra "Phuḥ" is recited. *Vajrakoṣam* means the vajra-club (*vajramuṣala*).

"By the impelling with the *phaṭ* mantra" means that one should impel [the deity] with a mantra distinguished by the syllable *phaṭ*, such as "Oṃ sumbha... and so forth. Regarding the reading "with the *phuḥ* mantra" and so on, according to the scripture (*āgama*) stating, "The mantra of the Horse-King is that of Vajrapātālaka," it refers specifically to the mantra of the Horse-King. [This is] the samādhi called "Anointing and Eye-Medicine Vajra. Then, having heard these words of the Blessed One, all the Tathāgatas were filled with joy and delight, and they spoke these words:

*Āmaho Vajra, Āma Vajra! The teaching of Āma Vajra is that all phenomena are empty; for it is within this emptiness of all phenomena—such as medicinal substances and the like—that the supreme siddhi is firmly established.* *śūnyeṣu sarvadharmeṣv iti bhaiṣajyādiṣu*
Just as a sweet fruit of essence may grow upon a plantain tree that has no core,
so too does the sweet fruit of siddhi arise from this body that has no core.
Space is the source of all things and the locus of all phenomena.
The mind is pure like the sky; a virtuous mind is supremely blissful.
Regarding "of all beings," this refers to living creatures. Regarding "all phenomena," this refers to [colors] such as blue and yellow. Here, the two words "as" and "so" are to be supplied.
By the nature of the ultimate sense-faculties, there is no external transformation apart from the mind.
"Form and so forth, which are asserted to be [external], should be understood as being the mind itself.

Then the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that while the mind of all Tathāgatas is empty, external objects are said to arise from the mind as non-empty? The Tathāgata replied:
Through the habitual tendencies of beginningless existence, external objects are conceptualized;
the mind conceptualizes everything, and the mind is said to be all-pervasive.
This is the samādhi called "The Vajra Teaching on the Emergence of the Bodhicitta."

"Extremely beautiful, with wide eyes, the source from which the *sihlaka* and *karpūra* arise— having brought her under control, he correctly begins by seizing her by the hair. Now, he speaks of the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*) with the words beginning "cāruvaktrām" (the one with the lovely face).
One should illuminate with the light of the vajra, press down with the attainment of the vajra, correctly take hold by embracing with the vajra, and press firmly with the lips of the vajra lady;
by means of the application of the vajra thumbs, one should thoroughly stimulate the vajra-abode.
By the emergence of Vajrasattva, one should truly consume him with the vajra tongue.

"Vajra-finger" refers to the hand-gesture (*mudrā*) and so forth; "vajra-abode" refers to the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*); "vajra-mind" [... "with the vajra tongue" means with the tongue marked by the vajra. Afterwards, one should cause Vajrasattva to enter that blissful state.
Through the yoga of the vajra-lord, one should properly perform the vajra-offering in the *dharmodaya* of Sukhāvatī. One should take up—that is, consume—the Vajrasattva-vajra.
Within the arising of Vajrasattva, the mind should be offered by one who is diligent.

With one possessing a lotus crest, one should worship with a red lotus. "Endowed with flowers" means suitable for the production of flowers. "With a red lotus" means with a lotus accompanied by [the quality of] service.
"The Vajra-holder adorned with a lotus" is distinguished by the red lotus.
By means of the application of the five products of the cow, the offering of a royal banner at the Gaṅgā will bring about diligence,
great bliss, strength,
and expansion; and by merely seeing it, this world will be brought under one's control.

"By means of the lotus" means by means of the lotus alone. "By the application of the five fragrances" means by the consumption of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). "By the worship with camphor on the banner" means either by the consumption of the *bodhicitta* itself.
Whoever has killed the Three Jewels, whoever has killed sentient beings, whoever has reviled the master, and those who have slandered the path of the Buddha—
"One should summon perfectly with the iron hook; bind the feet with the iron chain;
bind the neck firmly with the noose; and I, as the Vajra-being, shall summon.

To explain the means of subduing the wicked, he says "the Three Jewels," and so forth. "The Vajra-being shall summon" means that the Vajra-being, the yogin, shall summon—that is, bring under control—the one to be accomplished (sādhya).
"Should destroy" means "should kill. Having visualized the dakinis as Buddhas, one should offer them as the lord; by this, the Buddha-vīras and Vajrasattvas are slain.
"This is a great sin; it is the very nature of the Avīci hell.
This one will fall into the great hells. Having reflected thus, one should execute [the victim].
Then, having visualized the form of Vajra, one should meditate upon the expanse of space.

"Having been struck with the vajra-staff, one is born in the realm of the Vajra-holder. This means that the object of practice (*sādhya*), having been deceived [by the visualization], is born in the Akṣobhya world-system through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) exactly as described.
"If the hook and so forth are ineffective, one should also summon by means of food."
Having visualized the form by means of that very [mantra], one should establish it as the Vajra-maṇḍala itself.

Having demonstrated the power of the yogin who has attained mastery (*labdhasāmarthya*), the author states the procedure for another [type of practitioner] with the words beginning "if he is incapable" (*aśaktau*). This is the meaning here: when the yogin has not yet attained mastery, then, having made the Tathāgatas hear [the request], and having fashioned the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—such as a hook (*aṅkuśa*)—out of flour, he should rescue the object to be accomplished by means of those hooks and so forth fashioned from flour in the presence of those Buddhas. The phrase "he shall go to the realm of the Vajrin" (*vajriṇo bhuvanaṃ vrajet*) should also be applied here.
The king who speaks with a hook of iron, the one with the blue staff— his own name is the King of Power,
Trishūla (Three-Pointed), Acala (Immovable), and Khadgāgra-maṇḍala (Circle of Sword-Tips).
This is the samādhi called "Slayer of Great Conceptualization."
Then, the Vajradhara King requested that all [beings] be exhorted,
and for the purpose of protecting the samaya-vajra, he spoke of this hidden sphere of activity:
"The great beings, the Vajra Wrathful Ones, all have one face and two arms."
The left hand at the heart holds the thumb in the fist gesture, while the right brandishes one's own weapon.
He possesses the hook of the Slayer of Yama; the Invincible One has a vajra hook. Hayagrīva is supreme red; from the inseparable preparation of the nectar of accomplishment—
The King of Logicians is the Iron Hook; for Nīladanda, use his own name.
The King of Power is Trisūla; Acala is the Pinnacle of the Mandala of Syllables. For the King who Protects the Measure, meditate upon the Dharma Wheel.
Standing with the left leg extended beneath a vajra-topped wooden pillar,
one should meditate on Antaka (Yama) in the form of the blue Indra,
possessing a vajra that is invincible by others and resembling a moonstone that terrifies.
The great red wrathful one of Padma, the black sovereign of Vajrāmṛta,
and the great black wrathful ones of the boundaries; marked by the Holder of the Vajra upon their crowns,
they are Śrī Heruka himself, and Vajrasattva with his retinue.
Having beheld the wrathful deities of the lotus family, one should join with Vajrasattva;

abiding in the center of the vajra maṇḍala, one should meditate on the Vajrasūrya. "Abiding in the center of the vajra maṇḍala" means abiding in the center of the spokes of the protection wheel. "Vajrasūrya" refers to the solar maṇḍala.

Having visualized the lotus seats in the ten directions, one should thoroughly meditate upon the ten wrathful deities. As the very embodiment of the Wisdom Vajra, one is the lord of the fivefold mandala;
having visualized the māras beneath one's feet, one should meditate upon the five mandalas.
The protective wheel is of great majesty, blazing like the fire at the end of an eon;
revolving yet utterly unmoving, it is five hundred yojanas in size.
This is the samādhi called "The Vajra of Victory through the Power of the Samaya of Protection."

Then the Great Blessed One, abiding in the sequence of his own *adhiṣṭhāna*, shall explain from that very [state] through the yoga of his own *adhiṣṭhāna*: "In the center of the heart, there is a moon;
the reflection upon the moon is unobscured."
Completely pervaded by the light of the assembly of [deities], one should meditate on the vajra from that.
"In the heart" means in the center of the lotus and vajra; it is the unstruck *hūṃ* syllable.
One should meditate on the Vajranairātmyā Ḍākinī, exhorted by her dance.
One should visualize her as being about the size of a grain of barley, abiding at the end of the various ḍākinīs;
"by means of the vajra, Nairātmyā-ḍākinī. [This refers to] Nairātmyā characterized by the vajra. "Impelled by awakening" (bodhicodita) means between the two openings.
"Within the barley grain, all beings—the three realms, moving and non-moving"—
When one meditates in this way, one’s own blessings will be thoroughly accomplished.
Since forms, sounds, as well as smells, tastes,
and tangibles are not grasped by the yogi himself as objects of desire, there is therefore neither self nor other.

Regarding the term "desirable": because it is the object of desire, the *dharmodaya* is [called] "selfless" (*anātman*) from the perspective of another. As it says in the *Vajragarbha*: "Desiring the aspect of peaceful bliss, Without turbulence, without appearance, Without conceptualization, and without syllables."
"My own self does not perceive itself, having partaken even slightly of intoxication.
At the end of joy and the absence of joy, one completely abandons the net of conceptualization.

*Ātmeti* and *ātmanaḥ* [are used]; "it is not perception," because there is only the perception of pleasure. The word "as" (*yathā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "At the end" means in the middle.
Unchanging, transcending delusion, the Vajra of the Awakened Mind (Kye'i rdo rje) is vividly manifest;
non-material, he is Heruka in every aspect, completely surrounded by all the various forms.
He himself is the Protector Heruka, yet he does not recognize his own nature.
At that time, by means of the words "All-knowing" (*sarvajña*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fruit of meditative cultivation:
"The coming and going of beings was seen by him as if he were omniscient himself."
The Buddha and the sons of the Buddha, all the limbs and all the apertures, are fashioned like the threads of a net for the Lord.
Beholding the body as if it were non-existent, one assumes the form of the Vajra of the Instant; just as space is invisible, so too is this form.
"Without equal and unarisen, without clothing and without error; it is completely free from the five obscurations.
Regarding "free from the five obscurations," this means it is devoid of the five hindrances characterized by sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt.
Just as the reflection of a face in a mirror, once perceived, is devoid of pleasure,
so too does one clearly see the nature of oneself as Heruka.
That very reality exists as the objects, the sense faculties, and the aggregates, like the sky.

"The body is described as bliss itself, and it is not overcome by conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This means that it is not subverted by the nature of the conditioned, because this body has the nature of Heruka, who is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Form is not grasped by the eye, nor is sound by the hearer."
The taste is not perceived by the tongue, nor the scent by the nose;
the tangible is not grasped by the touch of the body.
Nevertheless, according to the manner of great bliss, it is more blissful than seeing a beautiful woman and better than the pleasure of hearing song.
Through the great bliss of smelling fragrances, the great bliss of touching the birth-place, and the application of drinking flavors—by what means could one obstruct that bliss?
Great bliss pervades all beings; those who do not realize bliss do not know it.
To the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, to the ḍākinīs and noble ladies,
and to the five Buddhas and the manifold [deities], may they awaken and become manifest;
"vibudhyatām" means "may they become manifest."
Then the great bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi spoke these words to the Blessed One regarding the Great Illusion:
"In order to subdue ordinary conceptualization, meditation is rightly renowned;
in order to subdue ordinary states, meditation is indeed non-meditation."
"Neither cultivation nor non-cultivation. The meaning is that the cultivation of a deity is not to be performed; once the form of the deity has been accomplished, what is the use of it?
"The Bodhisattvas understand it in this way; nevertheless, in order to purify the measure of impurity, one should meditate upon the image of the Tathāgata’s body.
Vajrapāṇi asked: "Bhagavān, what is the essential purpose of the method for cultivating embodied beings?"
The Blessed One said, "Guhyapati, there is a purpose.
[He asked,] "Blessed One, what is its name?
The Vajradhara replied, "It is Buddhahood itself."
"What is Buddhahood?
It is omniscience.
What is that? This embodied being is the truth."
Furthermore, why is that?
The Vajradhara declared:
"In this way, I am endowed with the thirty-two major marks and adorned with the eighty minor signs."
Why is that?
Because it is established as being dissimilar.
Vajrapāṇi asked:
"Bhagavān, are you well?
The Vajradhara replied, "I myself am the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna).
What is this mirror-like wisdom?"

The Vajradhara has commanded: it is not unreal, not false, not a cause, and not born. Thus, I myself am the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), I myself am the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), and I myself am the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). In this way, the expanse of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is utterly pure. Therefore, O Great Bodhisattva...
"Do not speak of that enlightenment as being devoid of aspects (*ākāra*);
for it is by way of a dissimilar cause— that is, by way of being empty of aspects—
that enlightenment is indeed without aspects."

"I am both existence and non-existence; I am declared to be the primordial Tathāgata. I possess the supreme form and formlessness, and I am endowed with the profound and peaceful Dharma. (api tu nirākārāpi tām eva darśayati | bhāvo 'ham ityādinā | gambhīreti | śūnyatārūpeṇa | udāreti | lakṣaṇādyalaṃkṛtena rūpeṇa |) Furthermore, although she is formless, she reveals herself in that very way through the words "I am existence" and so forth. "Profound" means by way of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Exalted" means by way of a form adorned with the [major] marks and so forth.
I am the great being Heruka, in union with Nairātmyā;
I am not insentient matter, born of great bliss; I am the sentient world of relative truth.
I truly pervade all five classes of beings— Men, women, and those of indeterminate gender.
Therefore, the Ocean of Victors has explained that which is called "the assembly.
Those who possess the vajra and the bodhisattvas are perfectly accomplished in the state of the neuter.
That goddess Nairātmyā is the consort of the essential nature.
I am the Buddha Heruka; for that very reason, I am not neuter.
Having perceived the two states of existence of wandering beings, I am the embodiment of skillful means and wisdom.
Through the yoga of supreme union, I am Akṣobhya, free from [ego] and devoid of selfhood.
This is the samādhi called "The Vajra Abode of Great Bliss, the Nature of the Sublime.
Then the Blessed One, the Great Hero, the Vajra of Desire, the Great Bliss, the Vajra Without Limbs, the Utterly Great Joy, spoke these words:
"Six-armed and accompanied by grace, with one face and wearing matted locks..."
The yellow one who has reached the age of sixteen accomplishes Vajrānaṅga;
in her right hand is an arrow, in her second hand a sword, and in the third it should be known as a mirror;
in her left hand is a bow.
Regarding the second [point], it is the state of supreme mastery; one should meditate on the six arms as the branches of the *kāmakellā*.
Having visualized [the consort] standing with her left leg extended at the heart of the maiden, the Vajra Queen will be accomplished.
*Madana*, *yis*, *o ma ’dzin pa ’big*, *a sho ka yis snying gar brab*, *ral gris skyes ma bsdig par bya*, *de nas me long bstan par bya*,
*gzhu yis rkang pa bcings nas ni*, *autpala zhags pas dgug par bya*.
Desiring that the hair be loosened and flowing, speaking with a most melodious voice,
performing the *ha* and *si* gestures,
joyful and adorned with well-proportioned limbs, the mouth filled with rows of teeth— thus one should contemplate her who is devoid of the power of desire.
Through the yoga of vajra worship, one should follow with an unchanging mind; without contrivance, the mantra of desire should be used to exhort that very heart.
Oṃ āḥ mu kī me kārṣāya manydzu ghoṣa hrīḥ dzaḥ.
By performing such meditation, the consort of Mañjughoṣa will desire the practitioner, bring him under her control, and come to him.
Through this practice for half a month, by means of ten thousand recitations, she will appear.
The moving golden-winged one, accomplished with a perfectly pure mind,
born from the seed-syllable *hāṃ*, and adorned with every ornament—
by means of the supreme application of drinking wine, one accomplishes the limbless Vajra.
The supreme seed-syllable for this purpose is by nature both pleasure and suffering;
it is great bliss, supremely peaceful, and brings joy to all sentient beings.
This is the great life-force, the beautiful one of supreme delight.
Bliss and suffering are always known through that mindfulness in such a way;
likewise for sorrow and passion, as well as joy and separation from joy.
O Great King Vajrasattva, that very reality is expressed as the six syllables.
Endowed with the half-moon, worshiped as the very essence of the unchanging bindu,
it is the *ālaya* of sentient beings and the excellence of all the tantras. Then,

having heard the syllable that is the seed of the Great Bodhicitta-vajra of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata of All Blessed Ones, the clarity of the realization of the mind was attained, and he spoke these words:
"There is no *sattva* and there is no meditation; there is no mantra and no deity.
Arising from the vajra of the mind—this is the firm stage of enlightenment.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajrasamaya.
"Without misfortune and without sin; without awakening and without a Buddha—through the application of the five primordial wisdoms, the bodhicitta is firm.
Thus spoke the Blessed One by means of the seal of the wheel.
There is no mantra recitation whatsoever, nor do the three realms of existence exist;
by the very nature of the dharmadhātu, there is neither meditation nor one who meditates.
Thus spoke the Blessed One with the precious samaya.
Relative worldly existence also exists; when analyzed, wherever one abides in the world, one always revolves within that very world.
This is the teaching on the stages of awakening.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Padma Samaya.
Unborn, unobservable, indivisible like space,
and profound and peaceful by nature— this is the gradual teaching on awakening.
Thus spoke the Blessed One with the pledge of the Sword.
"Just as an illusion, just as a mirror, just as space,
and just as bliss— this thorough knowledge of all things is the teaching on the stages of enlightenment.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lady, the ḍākinī Nairātmyā.
The stainless state of sublime emptiness, Which is the very nature of dreams and illusions— Until such time as it is exhausted, Meditate upon the nature of the mind!
Māmakī!
There is no birth and no nirvāṇa; this is the Great Bliss Vajra.
Whoever meditates by means of mental cultivation, that is the meditation of supreme cultivation.
O Locanā!
Free from mantras and letters, this is mindless and without the bindu;
it is that sublime great bliss, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This is Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
Just as a reflected image is by nature [empty], so should one meditate upon all things.
This is the supreme, stainless state of emptiness; now there is neither merit nor sin.
O Tārā!
"Just as the moon within water is neither real nor unreal, so too,
by means of the maṇḍala wheel, the nature of the body is stainless.
Thus spoke the entire assembly.
Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called "Victory over the Multiform Creator" and emitted this bow and arrow from his vajra body,
speech, and mind: "Holding the *muḥ* syllable and the yellow ear of grain with the right hand,
and holding the left thumb with the left hand of desire, one should bind and purify the various lines."
"Unstruck" (*anāhata*) refers to that which has the nature of the syllable *haṃ* and of pleasure and pain, because it is all-pervasive.
"Muccuṭī" refers to the contraction of all the fingers.

*Siṃhakarṇī* [is so called] due to the contraction of the index and middle fingers. *Sāyaka* means an arrow. *Vajra-vistaratām* means an extreme expansion due to arrogance. *Cakṣuḥ* refers to both eyes. *Kāminī* is the *priyaṅgu* plant. *Kaccoram* is *śaṭhī*. The word *keśa* means hair; *bolakam* is *gandharasa*. *Śālijam* is *khaṭṭāsa*. "In every way, by forceful means" (*sarvathā haṭhasādhanena*) means that in the practice of *haṭha*, incense should be offered using all these specific fragrances. "All those" (*sarve te*) means by means of all of them.

"With agitation" means with reverence. "In front of the graceful movements" means with grace; it refers to moving forward gracefully while following the tips of the playful gestures. "Eight steps" means for a distance of eight paces. "With eyes and hands" [refers to]: having turned the hand, one holds it above the ear like a *patākā* (banner) using the index and middle fingers. "With hips and hands" means circling clockwise with the feet, and "counter-clockwise" means turning to the left. "The shrine" (*caitya*)... [end of fragment].

With the left hand facing downward, one forms a fist with the thumb [of the right hand]. "By Vajrasattva" means by the syllable *hūṃ*. The "meditation on the lotus-vajra" is the manifestation of the lotus and the thunderbolt. "Of that, at the tip of the nose" means the filament of that lotus [is formed] by the syllable *āḥ*, [and] "by the *praṇavas*" means by the syllable *oṃ*. The "wish-fulfilling gem" is the thunderbolt-gem.
"Holding the hands in the *kośa* (folded) position, and holding the fist of the sword, one should discharge the arrow with *hūṃ* and destroy the mandala of the Māras."
Having drawn in the breath, one should fill the body with wind;
grasping the fists against the body, one should expand the chest. One should fix the mind upon the object of focus, and fill the mouth with the syllable *Hūṃ*.
By means of the union with G-yas-brkyang and so forth, one should slay the rākṣasa Yama.
What is the use of speaking much here? This is merely a summary according to conventional truth.
Whatever is the root of the science of archery, that is the conduct of the Vajradhara.

Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption known as “The Sound of Vajra Music,” and from the vajra body, speech, and mind of this very playfulness of the sound of music, he uttered these syllables:
*tha him tha him, thaka thaka, thuka thuka, thā hi thā hi, bā hi bā hi, au dhām au dhām, kāṃ ka kāṃ ka, thaka thaka, hī dhām hī dhām, ta dvā va ta dvā va tāṃ.*
The *cha-lang*, the drum, and also some clay drums, the *pi-wang* lute, the sweet-toned *ling-bu* lute, the three-stringed lute, and the *kāra-taka*—
these should be played by striking them in three ways; by playing them softly, one attains victory.
Regarding the request for the mandala and so forth: "This offering is unsurpassed;
what is the use of many of my own verses?
Whatever [is found] in the treatises on musical performance—that is the sound of the Vajra Dance."
Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called *Gandhavajra* (Fragrant Vajra) and emitted this very offering of incense from his body, speech, and mind-vajras:
"Sandalwood, *gur gum*, bitumen, and likewise *kāmā*—these substances are great incenses. Offer them well to Heruka. Also, *kaṭphala* and *kuṅkuma*..."

Likewise, these essences of incense—*śrī*, *śrī-ja*, *bhadra-kṛt*, and *sāra*—should be applied for the sake of benefit. *Kuṇḍuru*, *prathamaka*, *ṛkṣanābhi*, and *nakha*: this incense of the King of Jewels (*ratnarāja*) is taught by the Vajradhara as always providing fearlessness to all. *Kuruvinda*, *kuṅkuma*, *śrīvāsaka*, *śaśi*, *jāti*, and *śalika*: this incense of the Protector of the World (*lokanātha*) was spoken by the Vajradhara.

From the *Vividha-vajra-pūjā* (The Vajra Offering of Various [Substances]), regarding the fragrance specifically for the nose: this offering of the King of the Seven is the accomplishment of Universal Power (*Samantabala*). Whatever is taught in the treatises on fragrances—whether it be the supreme incense of the *duma* tree or any other—all these are renowned as the "Vajra Offerings" of Vajrapāṇi. Then, the Blessed One entered the samādhi called "The Array of the Vajra Steps."

"Like at the time of childbirth, by oneself" means that, for the sake of pacifying the suffering of those afflicted by the pains of labor, one should remain as if present at the time of birth oneself. "Desiring a lotus" refers to the longing for an ordinary lotus. "Having placed the Wielder of the Thunderbolt" means having introduced the *kuliśa* (thunderbolt). "And indeed the Fully Awakened One" (*saṃbuddha*)—because it has been accepted by the Fully Awakened Ones, the Flower Consecration (*puṣpābhiṣeka*) is called "the Fully Awakened One. "One should avoid the binding of the mudrās," and so forth; this is stated for practitioners of the *utpannakrama* (generation stage). "Those who are not teachers" means those who do not have a guru. Then the Vajra-holder King spoke these words to all the Buddhas and to the Yoginīs within the Vajra Pavilion: "One should visualize [the deity] who has two arms and one face, whose nature is born from the vajra, holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga in his hands; having visualized him, one should emanate and recite. White, red, and likewise blue, Vārāhī is joined in union with him. Red in color and four-armed, he is joined with Ekavaktrā and Vaśīkarī; he stands upon the seat of Vajradharma—this is what is called Kurukullā. This is the mantra.

The Exposition: Regarding the Queen Abiding in the Dharma, I shall now explain in full detail what I myself heard in the presence of Your Majesty at one particular time. Thus have I heard: at one time, in the presence of the Blessed One, the Queen’s Dharma was extensively proclaimed; [it includes] the gazing, the summoning, the great signs, and the performance of purposeful actions.

Born from the reality (*tattva*) of *Nus* and *Char*, the Great Sage, the Protector of the World, has two arms and one face; he is adorned with the gesture of generosity (*varada*) and a lotus, and is perfectly seated upon a lotus throne. His head ornament possesses the Vajra-Dharma. Born from the reality of *Mām*, Mañjughoṣa is yellow in color; his limbs are adorned with the gesture of generosity and an *utpala*. Akṣobhya-Vajra...

Holding the crown of the head, arisen from the wisdom of *hūṃ*, with the hand brandishing a sword in a threatening gesture, he stands upon the back of a great buffalo with his left leg extended. Having a wrathful form that inspires fear, he holds Akṣobhya in front of him with his hands joined. Arisen from the wisdom of *hūṃ*, the Vajra-hūṃ-kāra, the Vajra-holder, forms the mudrā with both hands through the union with the vajra bell.

With the left leg extended, one should visualize the body of the Subduer of Bhairava; having visualized the Vajra family upon the crown of the head, one should recollect Trailokyavijaya. Arising from the syllable *Tām*, it is the supreme weapon of the Lord of Offerings, like a goddess with a complexion like that of a blue lotus, always abiding in an excellent posture and perfectly seated upon a variegated lotus, holding the Amoghasiddhi at her crown.

One should meditate on the Great Beautiful One, the Fortunate Lady (Subhadrā), who has the form of Tārā. Arising from the syllable *Māṃ*, she holds an *aśoka* flower as an offering. She is like the rising sun, with the glory of Vairocana born upon her crown. Through the posture of her left leg extended, she crushes the chariot of the Seven Coursers. Adorned with the flavor of graceful limbs, one should meditate on her as radiant with light. At the navel...

From the syllable [Bāṃ] arises light like the autumn moon, abiding within a jewel *cintāmaṇi* at the heart; it remains perfectly seated in a beautiful manner. One should meditate on the goddess, who sits upon a lotus throne amidst a host of deities, her head bowed in devotion; she is the Bodhicitta flowing forth, a goddess devoid of worldly power. From the syllable Bāṃ arises the Earth-Goddess (*Dharaṇī*), intensely golden in color, with her hands—

From the vajra posture of the mudrā of offering, Adorned with the limbs that are the source of jewels, With eyes exceedingly beautiful, One should meditate upon the Queen of Yakṣas; She becomes identical to the Lord of Wealth (Jambhala). Arising from the syllable Dzaṃ, One should meditate on the one called Gaganagañja. Yellow in color, in her right hand Is the mudrā of offering, a jewel lion cub; [The other] is a jewel...

The one born from the *Byung gnas rdo rje* (Akṣobhya) should be visualized as adorning the crown of the head with a maṇḍala; one should imagine a rain of jewels falling. One should place the vajra-water at the height of the navel. From the syllable *Praṃ*, there arises a goddess, white in body and lovely to behold, holding a sword and a wheel, her crown pressed down by the *Phan pa* (Maitreya). It is like one's own [emanation] during a great multitude of times.

Seated correctly in the place of the maṇḍala, one should visualize Mañjughoṣa emerging from the expanse of space. Then, the Blessed One, the Great Vajra-holder, having absorbed all various mantras within himself, entered the meditative absorption called "Vajra" and uttered these mantra words: Oṃ mānī padme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ māṃ dzu.

"DI NA ME KE NA HŪṂ PHAṬ HŪṂ. Having fashioned an image of the three poisons, fill its body with red arsenic, wrap it in poison and human fat, and then, while reciting the name of whoever [is the target], burn it in fire. At that time, they will become invisible.

Furthermore, another excellent explanation follows: the very meditation on the siddhi of the mudrā is the great siddhi of the mudrā, which is not within the sphere of experience of all [ordinary] siddhis. At that time, one’s body is agitated, yet in one moment it is the manner of great bliss; in one moment, one possesses that retinue. Through meditation and mantra itself, in a single instant one becomes the Buddha Vairocana, embraced by the multitude of his eyes.

In an instant, one possesses non-duality; great joy and supreme rapture. In a single moment, the King who holds the Vajra unites with Māmakī in bliss. By offering at the tips of the vajra and lotus, in an instant one possesses non-duality. Through the excellent union of vajra and lotus, one transcends to the other shore with vajra devotion. One should offer the vajra and lotus, yet abandon the desire for the lotus. Oneself...

Making offerings for the sake of the siddhis of China, one thoroughly accomplishes Mahāmudrā; this is the samādhi called "The Vajra of the Power of Complete Victory. Accomplishment will be attained in a single day, or by the method of two days, or the application of three days, and likewise four days; through the application of five days, accomplishment will be achieved—of this there is no doubt. Having performed [the preliminaries], one should sit in the place of meditation. Having entered together with the mudrā, one should correctly engage in the vajra-yoga. This yoga should be correctly practiced at the time when the vajra-sun has set. At the time of sunrise, there is no doubt that accomplishment will be attained through the passion of great desire.

From the nature of great passion, abiding in the samādhi of great passion, one should thoroughly accomplish Mahāmudrā. This is the samādhi called "The Extremely Joyful Vajra. Having placed the lotus-holder [the consort] within, one should take one’s own vidyā as one’s mistress; together with her, one will achieve accomplishment. This is declared to be Mahāmudrā. Having taken the mudrā of a human woman, upon her [one should visualize] the wheel.

Having thoroughly distinguished [the offerings] and prepared them in accordance with perfumes and flowers, one should correctly arrange the wheel. Having prepared [the offerings] in accordance with the eyes, the self-mother Tārā, and the extremely captivating white goddess, through perfumes and flowers, one should correctly perform the vajra-worship. Through mantra, benefit shall be accomplished; the Vajrapāṇi-siddhi, the Vajrasūrya-siddhi, and the Siddhi of the Sublime Syllables shall be attained.

The seventh king, Siddha, and the All-Leader, Siddha, shall be accomplished. The water initiation is the first; the crown initiation is the second. This is the ninth [chapter] from the *Abhiṣeka*: Through the yoga of that very vajra, the reality of all is proclaimed by the practitioner; having been prophesied by the Teacher himself, this here is the ritual of empowerment. One must not disparage the preceptor, nor transgress the command of the Sugata. One must not disparage one’s own kin, nor harbor malice toward sentient beings. One must not abandon the bodhicitta, nor disparage the teachings of oneself or others.

Do not speak; do not speak of that very [nature] to those who lack the fortune. Do not disparage sentient beings who possess the fortune, nor disparage even your own body. Do not harbor doubt regarding the Dharma, and do not show affection toward the malicious. Do not attempt to measure the nature of reality (dharmatā). Constantly guard your samaya and do not disparage the Dharma of others. Do not disparage women either. This is the brief instruction on thoroughly abandoning the root downfalls.

This is the meditative concentration called *BA*. Until reaching the heart of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one must not forsake the Three Jewels. One should always maintain the commitments (*samaya*). One should also hold the vajra and the bell. One should always wear the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). One should always offer the fire sacrifice (*homāhuti*). One should always construct the maṇḍala. One should always perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the Sugatas. One should offer bali to the great spirits.

One should completely avoid giving gifts and binding mudrās; one must not perform the rites of a stūpa, nor offer homage to the supreme three vajras. One should not perform physical activities such as constructing maṇḍalas even in dreams, nor prostrate to other teachers. One should prostrate to the lineage of one’s own gurus. Constantly and perpetually recite mantras, never part from meditative concentration itself, and always gather in disciples.

Explain the field as being permanent; always nurture sentient beings; always honor the Buddhas; offer water to Jambhala; and correctly perform all ritual activities. Even for the activity of constructing a sand stūpa, the wise should act according to the prescribed procedure. Then, the Blessed One, together with all the bodhisattvas, all the male messengers, and all the female messengers...
Having heard this *Vajra-niścāraṇa* of all the Tathāgatas, he spoke these words: "You are everything for all sentient beings; you are the purifier of all sins; you have fully realized all phenomena."

Homage to the Vajradākinī. Beholding beings oppressed by hatred, In order to exhaust all delusion, The Victorious Lord Vairocana— Homage and praise to Delusion-Vajra! "PA NI: 'The one upon whom all Buddhas bestow their hands, our very own father and mother—this very person should be held in mind. Why is that? Because it was so commanded by the Tathāgata."

The siddhis of Vajrasattva Buddha, Vajradharma, Tejorāja, and the Seven Kings—since these are not attained through ordinary joy, but rather through the ointment for the eyes, foot-unguent, the accomplishment of the sword and the subterranean realm, the pill, the sky-farer, invisibility, and the extraction of essences—it is through the vajra of primordial wisdom and through devotion that they are swiftly obtained. That.

Therefore, having emerged from the state of the master, one pays homage to the Tathāgatas. Just as Vajrasattva is, so too does the master assume that form; having focused on the objective of sustaining sentient beings, he abides in an ordinary form. At the final time, the master declares: "This person has died; they have passed away into the non-abiding world—a birth that is base and deluded."

"By the conceptual thought called 'dying,' one is led to a pure realm; otherwise, one will certainly go to Sukhāvatī, or be born into a class of desire.
